title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Denmark: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Denmark: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Denmark: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the loss of your family member in Denmark. Navigating the medical, civil, funeral, financial, and probate procedures in Denmark follows a structured digital and judicial timeline, where hospital or municipal death reporting triggers automatic notifications to civil registries, banks, and the probate court. Below, we set out the 5 official steps in chronological order to help you manage the immediate formalities and estate administration.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or hospice death: When your family member dies in a Danish hospital, nursing home, or hospice, an attending physician conducts the external post-mortem examination (ligsyn) and completes the electronic medical death certificate (dødsattest) via the national health data system of Sundhedsdatastyrelsen [1] [3].
  • Death at home: If the death occurs at home and was expected, contact the deceased's general practitioner (egen læge) or the regional out-of-hours medical service (lægevagten) so a doctor can attend the residence, confirm the death, and issue the electronic dødsattest [1] [3].
  • Unexpected, sudden, or unexplained death: Under the Danish Health Act (Sundhedsloven), if a death is sudden, accidental, violent, or of unknown cause, the physician must notify the Danish police (Politiet), who coordinate a forensic medical examination (retslægeligt ligsyn) with Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed before releasing the body for burial, cremation, or international transport [1] [4].

steps.title: Complete Civil Death Registration and Obtain Official Certificates
steps.html:
• Automatic civil registry update: Once the physician submits the electronic dødsattest, the death is recorded automatically in the Central Person Register (Det Centrale Personregister - CPR), which immediately updates municipal records and notifies public agencies [1].
  • Filing the funeral and death request (Anmodning om begravelse eller bisættelse): Within 2 working days of the death (or as soon as practical before the 8-day burial deadline), next of kin or an authorized funeral director must submit the official registration and burial/cremation request digitally via Borger.dk using MitID (or by paper form if the notifier lacks Danish digital identification) [1] [2].
  • Registrar authority and certificates: The local parish civil registrar (kirkekontoret / begravelsesmyndigheden) in the deceased's parish of residence (or the municipal civil registry in Sønderjylland) processes the filing and issues the official death and person certificate (personattest with death annotation) in Danish and English upon request [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Statutory 8-day timeline: Under Danish law, burial (begravelse / jordfæstelse) or cremation (bisættelse) must generally take place within 8 days of death (counting the day of death), unless the local burial authority grants a brief extension for special family or logistical reasons [1] [2].
  • Licensed funeral director (bedemand): Families normally engage a licensed Danish funeral director (bedemand), who coordinates mortuary release once Page 1 of the dødsattest is signed, submits the burial application via Borger.dk, and books the cemetery or crematorium [1] [2].
  • International repatriation (ligpas and legalization): If the deceased's body or cremated ashes must be repatriated outside Denmark, Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed issues the mandatory international laissez-passer for a corpse (ligpas) once medical and forensic clearance, embalming, and a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin are verified [4]. If foreign authorities outside the EU require authentication of Danish civil status documents, Udenrigsministeriet provides the Hague Apostille or consular legalization on the official personattest [5].

steps.title: Notify Social Security, Pensions, Banks, and Claim Survivor Support
steps.html:
• Automatic account freeze and public notifications: When the death is registered in the CPR register, the deceased's bank accounts (including joint accounts), payment cards, NemKonto, MitID, and Digital Post are automatically frozen by financial institutions until the probate court issues an estate certificate [1] [6].
  • Funeral grant (begravelseshjælp) and survivor benefits: Udbetaling Danmark is notified automatically to stop state pensions (folkepension) and social benefits, and next of kin can apply digitally via Borger.dk for the means-tested statutory funeral grant (begravelseshjælp), supplementary labour-market pension lump sums (ATP Livslang Pension), and any survivor transition allowance (efterlevelseshjælp) [1] [2].
  • Tax and private policies: The Danish Tax Agency (Skattestyrelsen) receives automatic notice from the CPR system, while family members should directly contact private occupational pension funds, life insurers, trade unions (a-kasse), landlords, and subscription providers [1] [6].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Complete Probate (*Skifteretten*)
steps.html:
• Initial contact with Skifteretten: Following the death registration, the Probate Court (Skifteretten), a division of the local district court under Danmarks Domstole, sends a notice to the primary contact person listed on the burial request and schedules a telephone or in-person guidance meeting roughly 3 to 4 weeks after the death [1] [6].
  • Do not dispose of assets before the probate certificate (skifteretsattest): Until Skifteretten issues the official skifteretsattest, heirs must not empty the deceased's home, sell assets, divide personal belongings, or pay unsecured creditors, as premature disposal can make heirs personally liable for the deceased's debts [1] [6].
  • Forms of estate administration (skifteformer) and inheritance tax (boafgift): Depending on solvency and family structure, Skifteretten releases the estate under simplified low-value distribution (boudlæg for estates with net assets below the statutory threshold after funeral expenses), spousal retention of an undivided estate (uskiftet bo), private probate by solvent heirs (privat skifte), or court-appointed executor administration (bobestyrerbo) [6]. In private probate, heirs file an opening balance sheet (åbningsstatus) within 6 months and a final estate inventory (boopgørelse) to settle Danish estate and inheritance tax (boafgift and tillægsboafgift) [1] [6].
  • Cross-border estates and foreign heirs: Because Denmark has an opt-out from the EU Succession Regulation (Regulation 650/2012), Danish private international law governs estates domiciled in Denmark, and foreign heirs who lack MitID can execute a probate power of attorney (skiftefuldmagt) so a representative in Denmark can deal with Skifteretten and Udenrigsministeriet legalization requirements on their behalf [5] [6].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Denmark: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Denmark: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Denmark: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We understand how important it is to have clear, reliable guidance when your family member in Denmark is facing an advanced or life-limiting illness. Taking structured medical, legal, and financial steps while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity (habilitet) ensures that their treatment preferences are legally respected and that trusted representatives can manage banking, property, and public correspondence without interruption. Below, we set out the 5 official steps to complete in order under Danish law.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Hospice Services, and Terminal Medical Status
steps.html:
• Medical terminal declaration (terminalerklæring): Ask the treating hospital specialist or general practitioner (egen læge) to assess whether to issue an official medical terminal declaration (terminalerklæring) and coordinate an integrated palliative pathway (palliativ indsats) between the regional hospital and the municipality (kommune) [1].
  • Full prescription drug subsidy (terminaltilskud): Once a physician submits the application for terminaltilskud to the Danish Medicines Agency (Lægemiddelstyrelsen), the ill person receives 100% public coverage for all prescribed medications, as well as municipal home nursing (hjemmesygepleje), assistive medical equipment, and nutritional preparations under the Danish Health Act (Sundhedsloven) and Service Act (Serviceloven) [1].
  • Specialized palliative teams and hospice: Through a physician's referral, patients with complex symptom management needs can access specialized hospital palliative care teams or inpatient stays at a recognized Danish hospice covered free of charge by the public healthcare system, with clinical standards overseen by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed [1] [3].

steps.title: Register a Living Will (*Behandlingstestamente*) and Healthcare Preferences
steps.html:
• Binding advance directive (behandlingstestamente): While still mentally competent and aged 18 or over, your family member can register an official behandlingstestamente (which replaced the older livstestamente in 2019) digitally via Borger.dk or Sundhed.dk using MitID [1] [3] [4].
  • Scope of medical instructions: In the behandlingstestamente register maintained by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, the patient can legally refuse life-prolonging treatment (including cardiopulmonary resuscitation) if they become permanently incapable of making informed decisions and are either in a situation where recovery is impossible, severely and permanently incapacitated, or experiencing severe suffering caused by the treatment itself [3] [4].
  • Designating a relative for treatment consent: Within the same behandlingstestamente, the ill person can authorize their closest relative (nærmeste pårørende) to have the final say on refusing life-prolonging treatment or consenting to treatment under coercion if the patient later loses decision-making capacity, and doctors are legally bound by these instructions [3] [4].

steps.title: Execute a Future Power of Attorney (*Fremtidsfuldmagt*) and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• Creating a fremtidsfuldmagt while capacity is intact: Under the Danish Future Powers of Attorney Act (Lov om fremtidsfuldmagter), the ill person can appoint one or more future attorneys-in-fact (fremtidsfuldmægtige) for personal and financial matters by registering the document digitally in Fremtidsfuldmagtsregisteret via Tinglysning.dk and Borger.dk [2].
  • Mandatory attestation before the notary (notaren): A digital fremtidsfuldmagt is not legally valid until the grantor personally acknowledges it before a court notary (notaren) at a local district court under Danmarks Domstole while still of sound mind (within 6 months of digital registration; the notary can also visit the hospital or home if illness prevents travel) [2] [6].
  • Activation via Familieretshuset and immediate bank mandates: A fremtidsfuldmagt remains dormant until the grantor loses capacity due to illness, at which point Familieretshuset puts it into force based on a medical certificate (lægeerklæring) [2] [5]. Because activation takes time, the ill person should also set up an immediate ordinary bank power of attorney (bankfuldmagt) directly with their Danish bank and a digital reading/action mandate (Digital Fuldmagt) on Borger.dk so a trusted representative can assist right away [1] [2].

steps.title: Activate Caregiver Leave (*Plejevederlag*) and Sickness or Disability Benefits
steps.html:
• Paid compassionate caregiver leave (plejevederlag): Under Section 119 of the Social Services Act (Serviceloven), a family member or close friend who cares for a terminally ill person at home can apply to the municipality via Borger.dk for a statutory care allowance (plejevederlag), combined with a right to unpaid leave from their employer so the municipal allowance compensates for lost wages [1].
  • Critical illness insurance (kritisk sygdom) and pension disability cover: Check the ill person's occupational pension scheme and group insurance (often viewable via PensionsInfo) to claim tax-free lump-sum payouts for critical illness (visse kritiske sygdomme), sickness benefits (sygedagpenge), or disability pension benefits (førtidspension) [1].
  • Municipal practical and respite support: Apply through the municipal visitation unit (visitationen) for home care (hjemmepleje), relief care (aflastning), and coverage of necessary extra illness-related expenses (merudgifter) [1].

steps.title: Review the Will (*Testamente*), Beneficiary Designations, and Cross-Border Records
steps.html:
• Executing or updating a notary will (notartestamente): Under the Danish Inheritance Act (Arveloven), statutory forced heirship (tvangsarv) reserves 25% of the estate for a surviving spouse and children, while the remaining 75% (friarv) can be distributed by will. Signing a notartestamente before the notary at Danmarks Domstole ensures the will is centrally registered in Centralregisteret for Testamenter and automatically retrieved during probate [1] [6].
  • Reviewing pension and life insurance beneficiaries (begunstigelse): Because life insurance and pension payouts usually pass outside the probate estate directly to the designated beneficiary (nærmeste pårørende or a named individual), verify and update beneficiary clauses directly with each pension company and bank [1].
  • Cross-border assets and document authentication: If the ill person holds property abroad or if family members reside outside Denmark, remember that Denmark does not participate in the EU Succession Regulation; ensure foreign powers of attorney and civil documents are coordinated in advance and, where required for foreign authorities, authenticated with an Apostille from Udenrigsministeriet [6] [7].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Finland: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Finland: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Finland: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the loss of your family member in Finland. Navigating the administrative, funeral, social security, and estate inventory formalities in Finland is streamlined because medical death reporting automatically updates the national Population Information System, which in turn notifies tax and pension authorities. Below, we set out the 5 official steps in chronological order to help you manage the immediate arrangements and statutory estate deadlines.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Confirmation of Death and the Burial Permit
steps.html:
• Hospital or care facility death: When your family member dies in a Finnish hospital, health centre, or residential care home, an attending physician establishes the death, determines the medical cause of death, and issues the burial permit (homalupa / hautauslupa) together with the death certificate (kuolintodistus) [1] [2].
  • Death at home: If the death occurs at home, call the general emergency number (112) or the regional wellbeing services county (hyvinvointialue) on-call medical service immediately so paramedics or police can attend the residence and transport the deceased to a healthcare unit for a physician's examination [1].
  • Forensic investigation (oikeuslääketieteellinen kuolemansyyn selvittäminen): If the death was sudden, unexpected, accidental, caused by an occupational disease or medical procedure, or otherwise unclear, the Finnish police (Poliisi) and the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) conduct a medico-legal investigation before issuing the burial permit (hautauslupa) [1]. Note that the burial permit is issued as soon as the body is released, whereas the final cause-of-death statement (kuolemansyylausunto) may take longer without delaying the funeral [1].

steps.title: Complete Civil Death Registration and Obtain Official Certificates
steps.html:
• Automatic notification to the Population Information System: The healthcare unit automatically transmits the death notification (ilmoitus kuolemasta) into the Population Information System (väestötietojärjestelmä) maintained by the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto - DVV) [1] [2].
  • Ordering official certificates and family relations extracts (sukuselvitys): Next of kin do not need to visit a registry office merely to report a domestic death, but you must order an official extract from the Population Information System (virkatodistus) from Digi- ja väestötietovirasto (and from Evangelical Lutheran or Orthodox parish registries for periods prior to 1999) covering the deceased continuously from age 15 until death to establish the legal heirs for banking and the estate inventory [1] [2].
  • Multilingual extracts and international legalization: If the deceased was a foreign citizen or if certificates must be submitted outside Finland, Digi- ja väestötietovirasto issues multilingual EU standard forms or attaches a Hague Apostille, while the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland (Ulkoministeriö) handles diplomatic legalization for non-Apostille countries [2] [5].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Engaging a funeral home (hautaustoimisto) and obtaining hautauslupa: Once the physician issues the burial permit (hautauslupa), a licensed Finnish funeral agency (hautaustoimisto) can transfer the deceased from the hospital mortuary and coordinate coffin burial (arkkuhautaus) or cremation (tuhkaus) without undue delay [1] [2].
  • Cemetery rights and cremation ashes: Evangelical Lutheran parishes (seurakunta) are required by the Funeral Services Act (hautaustoimilaki) to provide a gravesite for any resident of the municipality regardless of religious affiliation (including non-confessional cemetery areas), and if the deceased is cremated, the ashes must be permanently interred or scattered with the landowner's permission within one year of cremation [1].
  • International repatriation (ruumiinkuljetuslupa): If the body is to be transported out of Finland for burial abroad, the funeral director coordinates embalming, sealing in a zinc-lined international transport coffin, customs documentation, and any consular laissez-passer or document legalization required through Ulkoministeriö and the destination country's embassy [1] [5].

steps.title: Notify Social Security (Kela), Pensions, Banks, and Claim Survivor Benefits
steps.html:
• Automatic public updates and Kela survivor benefits: Once the death is recorded in the Population Information System, Kela (The Social Insurance Institution of Finland), public earnings-related pension providers (työeläkelaitos), and the Tax Administration receive the update automatically [1] [3]. Surviving spouses or partners and children under 18 (or up to age 20 if studying full-time) should apply to Kela and the deceased's earnings-related pension provider for the surviving spouse's pension (leskeneläke) and orphan's pension (lapseneläke) [1] [3].
  • Funeral assistance (hautausavustus): Finland does not pay a universal social security funeral grant, but funeral assistance may be available from the deceased's employer, trade union, municipal social assistance (toimeentulotuki via Kela for low-income estates), or statutory military injury and accident insurance schemes [1] [3].
  • Managing bank accounts as an undistributed death estate (kuolinpesä): Finnish banks freeze the deceased's personal online banking credentials and payment cards once notified via the population register [1] [2]. However, a shareholder of the death estate (kuolinpesän osakas) can present the initial virkatodistus showing their family relationship so the bank can pay funeral invoices and urgent household bills directly from the deceased's account before the full estate inventory is completed [1] [2].

steps.title: Complete the Estate Inventory (*Perunkirjoitus*) and Inheritance Tax Filing
steps.html:
• Mandatory 3-month estate inventory deadline: Under the Code of Inheritance (perintökaari), the shareholder managing the estate (pesänilmoittaja) must arrange an estate inventory meeting (perunkirjoitus) within 3 months of the date of death (an extension can be requested from Verohallinto before the 3-month deadline expires if cross-border or complex assets require extra time) [1] [4].
  • Drafting the estate inventory deed (perukirja) and DVV shareholder confirmation: Two trustees (uskotut miehet) appraise and record all assets and debts of the deceased (and any surviving spouse) as of the date of death, attaching the complete chain of family relations certificates (sukuselvitys) and any will (testamentti) [2] [4]. You may also apply to Digi- ja väestötietovirasto for official confirmation of the shareholder data in the estate inventory deed (perukirjan osakastietojen vahvistaminen) to simplify bank and property transactions [2].
  • Submitting the perukirja to Verohallinto within 1 month: A copy of the signed perukirja must be filed with the Finnish Tax Administration (Verohallinto) within 1 month of the estate inventory meeting; Verohallinto uses the perukirja as the inheritance tax return to calculate each beneficiary's Finnish inheritance tax (perintövero) [1] [4].
  • Cross-border estates and the European Certificate of Succession: Because Finland applies the EU Succession Regulation (Regulation 650/2012), if the deceased owned property in another participating EU Member State or had heirs residing abroad, Digi- ja väestötietovirasto issues the European Certificate of Succession (eurooppalainen perintötodistus) upon application [2] [4].

cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Finland: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We understand how important it is to have clear, practical guidance when your family member in Finland is facing an advanced or life-limiting illness. Putting medical directives, continuing powers of attorney, caregiver support, and estate documents in place while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity (oikeustoimikelpoisuus) ensures their wishes are respected and avoids delays in managing banking, health records, and property. Below, we set out the 5 official steps to take in order under Finnish law.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Hospital Services, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Palliative care plan (palliatiivinen hoitosuunnitelma) and end-of-life care decision (saattohoitopäätös): Ask the treating specialist or physician in your regional wellbeing services county (hyvinvointialue) to draw up an individualized palliative care plan and, when appropriate, a formal end-of-life care decision (saattohoitopäätös) in consultation with the ill person and their family [2] [3].
  • Home hospital (kotisairaala) and hospice care (saattohoitokoti): Through the wellbeing services county, patients can receive specialized 24/7 home hospital nursing (kotisairaala), pain management, and assistive equipment at home, or inpatient care in a palliative ward or hospice, coupled with public health care user-fee caps (maksukatto) and Kela medicine reimbursement ceilings (lääkekatto) [3] [4].
  • Designating next of kin in patient records: Ensure the treating healthcare unit records the primary family contact (lähiomainen) and the patient's explicit consent for sharing medical information with designated family members [2] [3].

steps.title: Record a Living Will (*Hoitotahto*) and Healthcare Proxy in MyKanta (*OmaKanta*)
steps.html:
• Drafting and saving a hoitotahto in OmaKanta: Under the Act on the Status and Rights of Patients (laki potilaan asemasta ja oikeuksista 785/1992), a mentally competent adult can record binding advance healthcare instructions (hoitotahto) directly in the national digital health portal MyKanta (OmaKanta) at Kanta.fi using Finnish online banking credentials or a mobile certificate [2] [3].
  • Scope of medical treatment preferences: In the hoitotahto, the ill person specifies which medical interventions they consent to or refuse (such as mechanical ventilation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or artificial nutrition when recovery is no longer possible), as well as preferences regarding pain relief and symptom care; physicians and nursing staff across Finland view this entry directly in the Kanta patient data repository and are legally bound to respect it [2] [3].
  • Designating a medical surrogate (hoitotahtoon nimetty edustaja): Within the hoitotahto text in MyKanta (or in a written document signed and witnessed by two impartial witnesses), the ill person can also name a trusted proxy to interpret their treatment wishes and receive medical information if the patient later becomes unable to communicate [1] [3].

steps.title: Execute a Continuing Power of Attorney (*Edunvalvontavaltuutus*) and Digital Mandates
steps.html:
• Drafting an edunvalvontavaltuutus while capacity is intact: Under the Act on Continuing Powers of Attorney (laki edunvalvontavaltuutuksesta 648/2007), the ill person (valtuuttaja) can appoint an attorney-in-fact (valtuutettu), plus a substitute attorney (varavaltuutettu) and an impartial substitute (esteetön varavaltuutettu) for conflict-of-interest transactions such as property sales or gifts, to manage both financial affairs (taloudelliset asiat) and personal matters (henkilöä koskevat asiat) [1].
  • Strict witnessing requirements and confirmation by DVV: The edunvalvontavaltuutus must be signed in writing by the grantor in the simultaneous presence of two impartial witnesses (kaksi esteetöntä todistajaa) who are not related to the grantor or the appointed attorneys [1]. The document enters into legal force only when the grantor loses capacity due to illness and the attorney submits the original deed plus a medical certificate (lääkärinlausunto) to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto - DVV) for official confirmation (vahvistaminen) [1].
  • Immediate bank and Suomi.fi mandates (Suomi.fi-valtuudet): Because DVV confirmation of an edunvalvontavaltuutus only occurs after capacity is lost and takes processing time, the ill person should also grant immediate Suomi.fi e-Authorizations (Suomi.fi-valtuudet) for pharmacy, healthcare, and tax transactions, as well as a direct bank account mandate (tilinkäyttöoikeus or pankkivaltakirja) at their Finnish bank while still able to act [1] [2].

steps.title: Activate Sickness, Care Allowance, and Informal Caregiver Support
steps.html:
• Kela sickness and care allowances: Apply to Kela for sickness allowance (sairauspäiväraha), pensioners' care allowance (eläkkeensaajan hoitotuki) to help cover extra costs and assistance needs caused by progressive illness, and reimbursement for medical travel expenses and prescription pharmaceuticals [4].
  • Informal care support (omaishoidon tuki) and family caregiver leave: If a family member provides regular care at home, apply to the regional wellbeing services county for informal care support (omaishoidon tuki), which includes a taxable care fee (hoitopalkkio), statutory respite days (lakisääteiset vapaapäivät), and caregiver coaching; employed family members also have statutory rights under the Employment Contracts Act (työsopimuslaki) to negotiate temporary absence or informal care leave (omaishoitovapaa) with their employer [4].
  • Earnings-related disability pension (työkyvyttömyyseläke): If the ill person is of working age, coordinate with their occupational health physician and earnings-related pension provider (työeläkelaitos) or Kela regarding partial or full disability pension benefits [4].

steps.title: Organize the Will (*Testamentti*), Tax Planning, and Cross-Border Documents
steps.html:
• Formal requirements for a Finnish will (testamentti): Under the Code of Inheritance (perintökaari), a valid will must be executed in writing while the testator has full testamentary capacity and signed in the simultaneous presence of two impartial witnesses aged 15 or over who know the document is a will [5]. Keep the signed original in a secure, accessible location (such as a bank safe or with a trusted attorney) because Finland does not maintain a central public will registry [5].
  • Reviewing marital property (avio-oikeus), beneficiaries, and tax rules: Review any prenuptial or marital property agreement (avioehtosopimus registered with Digi- ja väestötietovirasto), life insurance beneficiary clauses (edunsaajamääräys), and advance gift or inheritance tax implications published by the Finnish Tax Administration (Verohallinto) [1] [5].
  • Cross-border estates and document legalization: If the ill person owns assets outside Finland or is a foreign citizen, they may include an explicit choice-of-law clause in their will under the EU Succession Regulation (Regulation 650/2012) selecting the law of their nationality, and if powers of attorney or civil documents must be recognized abroad, obtain a Hague Apostille from Digi- ja väestötietovirasto or diplomatic legalization from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland (Ulkoministeriö) [1] [5] [6].

closingQuestion: Could you let us know which wellbeing services county or municipality in Finland your family member lives in, and whether they have already prepared an edunvalvontavaltuutus or hold any cross-border assets, so we can tailor the exact steps for your situation?

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Iceland: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Iceland: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Iceland: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the loss of your family member in Iceland. Navigating the medical, civil registration, funeral, social security, and probate formalities in Iceland is centered around the District Commissioner (Sýslumaður), who oversees both the formal death notification and the administration of the deceased's estate (dánarbú). Below, we set out the 5 official steps in chronological order to help you manage the immediate procedures and statutory estate filings.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death (*Dánarvottorð*)
steps.html:
• Hospital or nursing home death: When your family member dies in an Icelandic hospital (such as Landspítali) or residential care facility, an attending physician confirms the death, completes the official medical death certificate (dánarvottorð) under the supervision of Embætti landlæknis (Directorate of Health), and transmits it electronically or in sealed paper form to the District Commissioner (Sýslumenn) [1] [6].
  • Death at home: If the death occurs at home, call the national emergency number (112) or the local healthcare centre (heilsugæslan) immediately so a physician and, where standard procedure requires, the police can attend the residence to verify the circumstances of death [1] [6].
  • Sudden, unexpected, or unexplained death: Under the Act on Death Certification, Autopsies, and Handing Over of Remains (Lög um dánarvottorð, krufningar og afhendingu líka nr. 61/1998), if a death is sudden, accidental, or of unknown cause, the police (Lögreglan) and forensic medical examiners conduct a medico-legal examination (réttarkrufning) before the District Commissioner (Sýslumenn) authorizes the release of the body for burial or cremation [1] [2].

steps.title: Complete Civil Death Registration and Obtain Official Certificates
steps.html:
• Reporting the death (andlátstilkynning) to Sýslumenn: Next of kin must formally report the death to the District Commissioner (Sýslumenn) in the district where the deceased had their legal domicile (lögheimili), either digitally via the Ísland.is portal using electronic ID (rafræn skilríki) or in person, submitting the dánarvottorð and preliminary information on known heirs (tilkynning um andlát og erfingja) [1] [2].
  • National Registry update (Þjóðskrá Íslands): Once Sýslumenn verify the dánarvottorð and register the death notice, they transmit the record to Registers Iceland (Þjóðskrá Íslands), which updates the National Registry and issues official multilingual death certificates (dánarvottorð úr þjóðskrá) and family certificates [1] [2].
  • Statutory reporting timeline: The death notice (andlátstilkynning) must be lodged before any funeral, cremation, or international transport of remains can take place, and Sýslumenn issue the funeral permit (jarðarfararleyfi) immediately upon registration [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Engaging a funeral director (útfararstofa): Families typically engage a licensed Icelandic funeral director (útfararstofa), who transfers the deceased to the mortuary (líkhús), collects the jarðarfararleyfi from Sýslumenn, and coordinates coffin burial (jarðsetning) or cremation (bálför) at the municipal cemetery (kirkjugarðar) [1] [2].
  • Cremation and interment rules: Under Icelandic cemetery legislation, cremations in Iceland take place at Fossvogur Crematorium (Bálstofan í Fossvogi), and cremated ashes must be interred in an approved cemetery plot or scattered over uninhabited land or sea with explicit permission from Sýslumenn [1] [2].
  • International repatriation and Apostille authentication: If the deceased was a foreign citizen or if remains must be repatriated abroad, Sýslumenn and Embætti landlæknis verify medical clearance, embalming, and a hermetically sealed zinc-lined transport coffin to issue the international corpse transit permit (líkvegabréf) [1] [6]. For foreign authorities requiring authenticated civil documents, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (Utanríkisráðuneytið) attaches the Hague Apostille to official certificates issued in Iceland [1] [2].

steps.title: Notify Social Security (Tryggingastofnun), Pension Funds, and Banks
steps.html:
• Automatic account freeze and national notifications: When the death is recorded in the National Registry, Icelandic commercial banks automatically freeze the deceased's personal bank accounts, debit and credit cards, and online banking access until Sýslumenn issue an official estate certificate (yfirlýsing um skipti) [1] [5]. However, banks permit documented funeral invoices (útfararkostnaður) to be paid directly out of the deceased's bank balance [1].
  • Survivor benefits (dánarbætur) and funeral grants (útfararstyrkur): Tryggingastofnun (Social Insurance Administration) is notified via the National Registry to adjust or cease state pensions, and surviving spouses or cohabiting partners with children under 18 can apply via Ísland.is and Tryggingastofnun for statutory bereavement benefits (dánarbætur) and child pension payments (barnalífeyrir) [4]. In addition, most Icelandic mandatory occupational pension funds (lífeyrissjóðir) pay a surviving spouse's pension (makalífeyrir) and trade unions (stéttarfélög) pay a substantial lump-sum funeral grant (útfararstyrkur) upon presentation of funeral receipts [1] [4].
  • Tax transition to the death estate (dánarbú): Skatturinn (Iceland Revenue and Customs) automatically closes the deceased's personal tax period on the date of death and establishes the dánarbú as a separate taxable entity until estate settlement is completed [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Complete Probate (*Skipti á dánarbúi*)
steps.html:
• Mandatory 4-month deadline to declare estate settlement: Under the Icelandic Estate Administration Act (Lög um skipti á dánarbúum o.fl. nr. 20/1991), heirs must notify Sýslumenn within 4 months of the date of death how the estate (dánarbú) will be administered [1] [2] [3].
  • Four statutory forms of estate settlement: Depending on the deceased's assets, liabilities, and family situation, Sýslumenn authorize one of four procedures: (1) closure due to no assets (eignalaust dánarbú) when assets only cover funeral expenses; (2) permit for a surviving spouse to retain an undivided estate (seta í óskiptu búi); (3) private probate by the heirs (einkaskipti), where heirs assume liability for the estate's obligations and receive the leyfi til einkaskipta; or (4) official court-supervised division (opinber skipti) through the District Court (héraðsdómur) if heirs disagree or the estate is insolvent [1] [2] [3].
  • Filing the inheritance report (erfðafjárskýrsla) and paying inheritance tax (erfðafjárskattur): In a private settlement (einkaskipti), heirs (or a designated representative holding a power of attorney for the estate, umboð vegna einkaskipta) must submit the final inheritance report (erfðafjárskýrsla) and tax return for the estate to Sýslumenn and Skatturinn within 1 year of obtaining the private probate permit, paying the 10% statutory inheritance tax (erfðafjárskattur) on net inherited value above the tax-free threshold (surviving spouses and registered cohabiting partners with a mutual will are exempt) [1] [3] [5].
  • Cross-border estates and foreign heirs: Because Iceland is an EEA state outside the EU Succession Regulation, Icelandic private international law governs estates domiciled in Iceland; heirs residing abroad who lack Icelandic electronic ID can sign a witnessed estate power of attorney (umboð til einkaskipta) legalized with an Apostille so a representative in Iceland can complete the filings with Sýslumenn and Skatturinn [1] [3] [5].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Iceland: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Iceland: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Iceland: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We understand how important it is to have clear, reliable guidance when your family member in Iceland is facing an advanced or life-limiting illness. Putting palliative care plans, advance medical directives, continuing powers of attorney, and estate arrangements in place while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity (lögræði) ensures their treatment preferences are legally respected and allows trusted family members to handle banking, benefits, and property seamlessly. Below, we set out the 5 official steps to complete in order under Icelandic law.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care (*Líknandi meðferð*), Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Specialized palliative care and home nursing (heimahjúkrun): Ask the treating hospital physician or local healthcare centre (heilsugæslan) for a referral to the specialized palliative care team (líknarráðgjafarteymi at Landspítali or Akureyri Hospital), the palliative care ward (líknardeild), or the round-the-clock specialized home nursing service Heimahlynning [1] [4].
  • Co-payment ceilings and prescription drug coverage: Ensure the treating physician submits necessary medical certificates (læknisvottorð) to Sjúkratryggingar Íslands (Icelandic Health Insurance) so the ill person benefits from statutory co-payment caps (greiðsluþátttökukerfi), full subsidies for essential palliative medications (lyfjaskírteini), and coverage for medical aids and assistive equipment (hjálpartæki) at home [4].
  • Recording the primary family representative: Under the Icelandic Patients' Rights Act (Lög um réttindi sjúklinga nr. 74/1997), confirm that the ill person's primary next of kin (nánasti aðstandandi) is explicitly recorded in the electronic medical chart and authorized via the Heilsuvera patient portal to receive clinical updates [1].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Directives in *Lífsskrá* and Heilsuvera
steps.html:
• Registering end-of-life treatment wishes in Lífsskrá: While mentally competent and aged 18 or over, your family member can log into the national health portal Heilsuvera (supervised by Embætti landlæknis, the Directorate of Health) using Icelandic electronic ID (rafræn skilríki) to record their advance medical directive in Lífsskrá [1].
  • Scope of medical instructions: In Lífsskrá, the patient documents their binding clinical wishes regarding end-of-life care (lífslokameðferð), including whether to withhold life-prolonging interventions or cardiopulmonary resuscitation if recovery is no longer medically possible and the patient has lost the ability to express their wishes; healthcare professionals across Iceland can access Lífsskrá directly in the national electronic health record [1].
  • Organ donation preferences (líffæragjöf): Within the same Heilsuvera portal overseen by Embætti landlæknis, the ill person can also verify or update their personal declaration regarding organ and tissue donation [1].

steps.title: Execute a Continuing Power of Attorney (*Vedurfarandi umboð*) and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• Drafting a continuing power of attorney (vedurfarandi umboð) while capacity is intact: Under the Icelandic Legal Competence Act (Lögræðislög nr. 71/1997, as amended to introduce vedurfarandi umboð), a mentally competent adult can execute a written continuing power of attorney appointing one or more trusted representatives (umboðsmenn) to handle personal and financial affairs if the grantor later loses capacity due to severe illness [2].
  • Witnessing and confirmation by Sýslumenn: The vedurfarandi umboð must be signed by the grantor in the simultaneous presence of two impartial witnesses (vottar) who certify the grantor's mental capacity, or acknowledged before the District Commissioner (Sýslumenn) [2]. When the illness later renders the grantor unable to manage their own affairs, the appointed representative submits the original document together with a physician's certificate (læknisvottorð) to Sýslumenn, who officially confirm and register the mandate so it enters into legal force [2].
  • Immediate digital mandates (umboð á Ísland.is) and bank powers of attorney: Because a vedurfarandi umboð only takes effect after Sýslumenn confirm incapacity, the ill person should also grant immediate digital authorizations in the Ísland.is mandate system (umboðskerfi Ísland.is) and execute a standard bank power of attorney (bankaumboð or allsherjarumboð) directly with their Icelandic commercial bank while still able to act [2] [3].

steps.title: Activate Sickness, Disability, and Spouse or Caregiver Allowances
steps.html:
• Tryggingastofnun disability and care benefits: Apply through the Mínar síður portal of Tryggingastofnun (Social Insurance Administration) for rehabilitation pension (endurhæfingarlífeyrir), disability pension (örorkulífeyrir), or age-related and illness-related expense supplements (uppbót vegna sjúkrakostnaðar), as well as spouse care benefits (maka- og umönnunarbætur) when a partner provides intensive home care [3].
  • Sjúkratryggingar Íslands sickness per diem (sjúkradagpeningar) and patient travel: If the ill person has exhausted paid sick leave from their employer, apply to Sjúkratryggingar Íslands for statutory daily sickness benefits (sjúkradagpeningar) and travel expense subsidies when travelling between regions for specialized treatment [4].
  • Trade union sickness funds (sjúkrasjóðir) and occupational pension disability cover: In Iceland, labour union sickness funds (sjúkrasjóðir stéttarfélaga) pay generous income-replacement grants during serious illness and grants for family caregiver absence, while mandatory occupational pension funds (lífeyrissjóðir) provide disability pensions (örorkulífeyrir) and critical illness insurance payouts [3] [4].

steps.title: Review the Will (*Erfðaskrá*), Marital Property, and Cross-Border Documents
steps.html:
• Formal requirements for an Icelandic will (erfðaskrá): Under the Icelandic Inheritance Act (Erfðalög nr. 8/1962), a testator with lineal descendants (niðjar) or a spouse is subject to forced heirship (skylduerfðir covering two-thirds of the net estate), while one-third (frjáls ráðstöfunarhluti) may be bequeathed freely by will [5] [6]. To be legally valid, the erfðaskrá must be signed or acknowledged by the testator while of sound mind before a notary public (lögbókandi at Sýslumenn) or two impartial testamentary witnesses (skírnarvottar / erfðaskrárvottar) who sign simultaneously and attest to the testator's mental capacity [2] [5] [6].
  • Mutual spousal arrangements and undivided estate consent: Married couples or qualifying cohabiting partners should review whether to execute a mutual will (gagnkvæm erfðaskrá) or pre-authorize the surviving partner to retain an undivided estate (seta í óskiptu búi) with Sýslumenn [2] [5] [6].
  • Cross-border estates and document legalization: Because Iceland is outside the EU Succession Regulation, if the ill person holds real estate or bank accounts abroad or has foreign heirs, coordinate local estate planning in each jurisdiction where assets are located, and have any powers of attorney used outside Iceland notarized by Sýslumenn and authenticated with a Hague Apostille by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (Utanríkisráðuneytið) [2] [5].

closingQuestion: Could you let us know which municipality or District Commissioner (Sýslumaður) district in Iceland your family member lives in, and whether they have already prepared a vedurfarandi umboð or hold any assets outside Iceland, so we can tailor the exact steps for your situation?

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Czechia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Czechia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Czechia: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Czechia. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order - covering medical certification, civil registration, funeral and repatriation formalities, social security notifications, and court-supervised notarial succession proceedings under Czech law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death (*List o prohlídce zemřelého*)
steps.html:
• Hospital or inpatient care facility deaths: When a death occurs in a hospital, hospice, or residential facility in Czechia, the attending physician conducts the mandatory post-mortem examination (prohlídka těla zemřelého) and completes the official Report on the Examination of the Deceased (List o prohlídce zemřelého) [1]. The healthcare provider notifies the close family, transfers the body to the facility's mortuary, and transmits the statutory parts of the examination report to the local civil registry office (matriční úřad) and the Institute of Health Information and Statistics [1].
  • Deaths at home or outside a medical facility: If your family member dies at home, call the emergency medical service (155 or 112) or the designated regional coroner service (koroner) so an examining physician can confirm the death on site and issue the examination report [1]. Once the physician clears the body for removal, your chosen funeral service (pohřební služba) can transport the deceased to a cooling facility.
  • Unexpected, sudden, or forensic deaths: If the death occurred suddenly, outside medical supervision, or under unclear or potentially external circumstances, the examining physician or the Police of the Czech Republic (Policie České republiky) orders a pathological-anatomical, health, or forensic autopsy (pitva) before burial or cremation clearance is issued [1].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Civil Registry (*Matriční úřad*)
steps.html:
• Competent authority and statutory deadline: Under Czech Act No. 301/2000 Coll. on Civil Registries, Name and Surname, the death is registered in the Book of Deaths (kniha úmrtí) by the municipal civil registry office (matriční úřad) responsible for the district where the death occurred [1]. The examining physician or healthcare provider must report the death to the registry office within three working days of knowing of the death (or completion of an autopsy) [1].
  • Documents to submit: Usually handled directly with the assistance of your commissioned funeral service, you must submit the deceased's Czech citizen identity card (občanský průkaz) or foreign passport/residence permit, birth certificate (rodný list), marriage or registered partnership certificate (oddací list) if applicable, and public health insurance card (průkaz pojištěnce) [1].
  • Official Death Certificate (Úmrtní list): Once recorded in the civil registry and the Basic Register of Inhabitants (Základní registr obyvatel), the registry office issues the official Death Certificate (úmrtní list) to the bereaved family and notifies the competent district court and public health insurer [1]. Additional certified copies or multilingual EU standard forms can be requested at any Czech POINT office or via the Public Administration Portal (Portál veřejné správy) [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Engaging a licensed funeral operator (Pohřební služba): Under Czech Act No. 256/2001 Coll. on Funeral Services, the transport, preparation, inhumation, or cremation of human remains must be carried out by a licensed funeral service [1] [2]. You are free to select any licensed funeral provider regardless of which transport service initially moved the body.
  • Burial and cremation permits: Burial in a cemetery (uložení do hrobu nebo hrobky) or cremation (zpopelnění v krematoriu) may proceed once both medical parts of the Report on the Examination of the Deceased confirm that no autopsy is required (or that the autopsy has concluded) and, where forensic investigation was opened, written consent has been granted by the police or public prosecutor [1].
  • International repatriation and document legalisation: If your family member's remains must be transported across borders, the funeral operator obtains a mortuary passport (umrlčí průvodní list) from the Regional Hygiene Station (Krajská hygienická stanice) or consulate and seals the remains in an approved zinc-lined coffin [1]. For civil status documents used abroad, EU Member States accept the Czech death certificate accompanied by a multilingual standard form under Regulation (EU) 2016/1191, while non-EU destinations require an Apostille from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (or Ministry of Justice for judicial/notarial documents) or consular superlegalisation [1].

steps.title: Notify Authorities and Claim Funeral and Survivor Benefits
steps.html:
• State funeral grant (Pohřebné): Administered by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (Ministerstvo práce a sociálních věcí) through the regional branches of the Labour Office of the Czech Republic (Úřad práce České republiky), the statutory one-off funeral grant of CZK 5,000 is payable to the person who arranged the funeral of a dependent child or of the parent of a dependent child, provided the deceased had permanent residence in Czechia [2] [3]. The application must be filed within one year of the date of burial using the funeral invoice and death certificate [2].
  • Survivor pensions (Pozůstalostní důchody): File applications for a widow's or widower's pension (vdovský nebo vdovecký důchod) and orphan's pension (sirotčí důchod) with the Czech Social Security Administration (Česká správa sociálního zabezpečení - ČSSZ) in person at any district office (OSSZ) or online via the ePortal of the Czech Social Security Administration [4] [5]. Widow's and widower's pensions are paid for one year after the spouse's death and continue thereafter if statutory age, disability, or dependent-care conditions are met [4].
  • Health insurance, banks, tax, and contracts: Return the deceased's health insurance card and any loaned medical aids to their health insurance company (zdravotní pojišťovna) within eight days, notify Czech banks to freeze sole accounts pending probate while checking any joint or designated-beneficiary accounts, and update utilities, telecommunications, and municipal tax records [1] [4].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Succession Proceedings (*Pozůstalostní řízení*)
steps.html:
• Automatic court initiation and notary assignment: In Czechia, heirs do not need to file a court petition to initiate probate [1]. Upon receiving the death notification from the civil registry, the district court (okresní soud) for the deceased's last permanent residence automatically opens succession proceedings (pozůstalostní řízení) and appoints a notary (notář) registered with the Notarial Chamber of the Czech Republic (Notářská komora České republiky) to act as court commissioner (soudní komisař) under a pre-set court rotation schedule [1] [6].
  • Preliminary inquiry (Předběžné šetření) and estate inventory: The assigned notary contacts the person who arranged the funeral for the preliminary investigation to identify statutory and testamentary heirs, inspect the Central Register of Wills (Evidence právních jednání pro případ smrti), and compile the deceased's assets (bank accounts, real estate in the cadastre, vehicles, securities) and liabilities [1] [6]. If the estate holds no assets or only assets of negligible value, the notary releases those minor assets to the funeral arranger and discontinues proceedings [1].
  • Succession resolution, tax rules, and cross-border estates: Following the final succession hearing, the notary issues a court resolution on inheritance (usnesení o dědictví) enabling asset transfers and land registry updates; inheritance acquired through succession is exempt from personal income tax in Czechia, though statutory notarial fees apply based on the net value of the estate [1] [6]. Where assets or heirs span multiple EU countries, the notary applies EU Succession Regulation (EU) No 650/2012 and can issue a European Certificate of Succession (Evropské dědické osvědčení) [1] [6].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Czechia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Czechia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Czechia: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Czechia is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, organising medical care, advance treatment preferences, legal representation, and financial benefits while the ill person retains full decision-making capacity ensures their wishes are respected. Below, we set out the five main official steps in chronological order under Czech law.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Insurance Coverage
steps.html:
• Specialist palliative and hospice care referrals: Ask your family member's attending specialist or registering general practitioner (praktický lékař) for a referral to an inpatient hospice (lůžkový hospic), a hospital palliative care team, or a mobile specialised palliative care provider (mobilní specializovaná paliativní péče) [1] [2]. In Czechia, medical palliative and home nursing services (domácí zdravotní péče) prescribed by a physician are reimbursed through mandatory public health insurance (Všeobecná zdravotní pojišťovna - VZP or departmental health insurers) [1].
  • Integrated social care services: For daily personal assistance, hygiene, and household support alongside medical nursing, arrange registered social care services (pečovatelská služba or osobní asistence) accredited under Czech Act No. 108/2006 Coll. on Social Services, which can be financed using the statutory Care Allowance [1] [2].
  • Medical equipment and home adaptations: Your family member's physician or palliative care provider can prescribe home medical aids (zdravotnické prostředky), such as adjustable beds, oxygen concentrators, and mobility aids, covered by public health insurance or supported through special aid grants from the Labour Office of the Czech Republic (Úřad práce České republiky) [1] [2].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Directives (*Dříve vyslovené přání*) and Medical Proxies
steps.html:
• Statutory advance directive (Dříve vyslovené přání): Under Section 36 of Czech Act No. 372/2011 Coll. on Health Services, an adult patient with full legal capacity may record an advance healthcare directive consenting to or refusing specific future medical treatments should they become unable to express their wishes [1] [5]. To be legally binding, the directive must be in writing, must be preceded by a written medical explanation from a physician regarding the consequences of the decision, and must bear an officially verified signature (úředně ověřený podpis) at a Czech POINT office or before a notary [1] [5].
  • Directive recorded directly during hospitalisation: Alternatively, your family member may record their advance treatment preferences directly into their medical chart upon admission to a hospital or hospice; this entry must be signed by the patient, the attending physician, and one witness [1].
  • Designating a surrogate decision-maker and access to medical records: Under the Health Services Act and the Czech Civil Code, your family member can explicitly designate a trusted person (osoba určená pacientem) in their medical documentation who is authorised to inspect health records, receive confidential clinical updates, and grant or refuse consent to healthcare interventions if the patient loses capacity and no advance directive covers the situation [1] [5].

steps.title: Execute Financial and Legal Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• General and special powers of attorney (Plná moc): While your family member retains full legal capacity (svéprávnost), prepare a written power of attorney under the Czech Civil Code empowering a trusted representative to deal with public authorities, tax offices, postal services, and property administration [5] [6]. For transactions requiring high legal certainty or real estate dealings with the Czech Office for Surveying, Mapping and Cadastre, have the signature officially verified at a Czech POINT counter or execute the mandate as a notarial deed (notářský zápis) before a notary registered with the Notarial Chamber of the Czech Republic (Notářská komora České republiky) [6].
  • Preventive guardianship declaration (Předběžné prohlášení): Under Sections 38 to 44 of the Czech Civil Code, an adult anticipating a future loss of capacity may execute a preventive declaration (předběžné prohlášení) - either as a notarial deed or signed before two disinterested witnesses - specifying how their affairs should be managed and who should be appointed as guardian if a court ever needs to restrict capacity [6].
  • Bank account disposal rights (Dispoziční právo): Czech banks generally require their own internal account mandate forms rather than a general civil power of attorney. Arrange for your family member to register an authorised account user (disponent) via online banking, at a branch, or through a mobile notary visit, and clarify with the bank which mandates remain valid if capacity declines [5] [6].

steps.title: Activate Care Allowance, Disability Pensions, and Caregiver Benefits
steps.html:
• Care Allowance (Příspěvek na péči): If your family member requires regular assistance from another person in basic daily life needs due to a long-term unfavourable health condition, apply for the Care Allowance via the Public Administration Portal (Portál veřejné správy) or at the regional branch of the Labour Office of the Czech Republic under the oversight of the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (Ministerstvo práce a sociálních věcí) [1] [2]. The benefit is graded across four dependence levels (Grades I to IV) following a social inquiry and medical assessment [1].
  • Disability pension (Invalidní důchod): Where the illness reduces working capacity by at least 35 percent (tiered into first, second, and third degree disability), file a disability pension claim with the Czech Social Security Administration (Česká správa sociálního zabezpečení - ČSSZ) either at a district office (OSSZ) or online through the ePortal of the Czech Social Security Administration [2] [3] [4].
  • Long-term caregiver allowance (Dlouhodobé ošetřovné): Employed family members who provide home care following at least a four-day hospitalisation or for an incurable palliative condition requiring terminal care can claim Long-Term Caregiver Allowance (dlouhodobé ošetřovné) from the Czech Social Security Administration for up to 90 calendar days, with statutory job protection during the care period [2] [4].

steps.title: Review the Will, Civil Status Records, and Cross-Border Estate Planning
steps.html:
• Drafting and registering a valid will (Závěť): While Czech law permits holographic (handwritten) wills and wills signed before two witnesses, executing the will as a notarial deed with a notary of the Notarial Chamber of the Czech Republic ensures immediate registration in the Central Register of Wills (Evidence právních jednání pro případ smrti) so it is automatically located during future probate [5] [6]. Keep in mind that under the Czech Civil Code, descendants are forced heirs (nepominutelní dědicové) entitled to a compulsory share (three-quarters of their statutory share for minor children and one-quarter for adult children) unless statutory grounds for disinheritance apply [5] [6].
  • Consolidating civil and property records: Assemble your family member's citizen ID, birth and marriage certificates, real estate title extracts, pension decisions, and life insurance policies (checking whether insurance contracts name a specific beneficiary obmyšlená osoba, which pays out outside succession proceedings) [5].
  • Cross-border coordination: If your family member holds foreign nationality, has family members living abroad, or owns assets in another country, consult a Czech notary on including an explicit choice-of-law clause under EU Succession Regulation (EU) No 650/2012 and obtaining Apostilles on powers of attorney intended for cross-border use [5] [6].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Slovakia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Slovakia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Slovakia: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Slovakia. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order - covering medical certification, civil registration, funeral and repatriation formalities, social security notifications, and notarial succession proceedings under Slovak law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or residential care facility deaths: When a death occurs in a hospital, clinic, or inpatient care institution in Slovakia, the attending physician conducts the mandatory post-mortem examination (prehliadka mŕtveho tela) and issues the official Report on the Examination of the Deceased and Statistical Report on Death (List o prehliadke mŕtveho a štatistické hlásenie o úmrtí) [1]. The healthcare facility transmits the documentation electronically or directly to the competent local registry office (matričný úrad) and releases the body to your licensed funeral service after statutory cooling and examination intervals are met [1].
  • Deaths at home or outside a medical facility: If your family member dies at home, contact the emergency medical service (155 or 112) so an examining physician designated by the Health Care Surveillance Authority (Úrad pre dohľad nad zdravotnou starostlivosťou - ÚDZS) can perform the external medical examination at the place of death and issue the examination report [1].
  • Unexpected, sudden, or forensic deaths: Where the cause of death is unclear, sudden, or potentially linked to an external event, the examining physician or the Police Force (Policajný zbor) orders a forensic or pathological-anatomical autopsy through the Health Care Surveillance Authority before burial or cremation clearance can be granted [1].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Civil Registry (*Matričný úrad*)
steps.html:
• Competent authority and statutory timeline: Under Slovak civil registry rules administered under the oversight of the Ministry of Interior of the Slovak Republic (Ministerstvo vnútra Slovenskej republiky), a death is registered in the Death Book (kniha úmrtí) by the local registry office (matričný úrad) responsible for the municipality or city district where the death occurred [1]. The examining doctor must notify the registry office within three working days of the post-mortem examination (or upon completion of a forensic autopsy) [1].
  • Documents required for registration: Either a close relative or your authorised funeral provider submits the medical examination report along with the deceased's Slovak identity card (občiansky preukaz), birth certificate (rodný list), marriage certificate (sobášny list) if applicable, and health insurance card [1]. If the deceased was a foreign citizen, their passport and residence permit must be presented [1].
  • Issuance of the official Death Certificate (Úmrtný list): Once recorded, the registry office issues the first official Death Certificate (úmrtný list) free of charge and forwards the deceased's cancelled identity document to the police [1]. Additional official extracts or multilingual standard forms for use within the European Union can be requested in person or online through the Central Public Administration Portal (Ústredný portál verejnej správy) using an electronic identity card [1] [4].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Engaging a licensed funeral service (Pohrebná služba): Under Slovak Act No. 131/2010 Coll. on Funeral Services, transport, preparation, burial, and cremation must be performed by a licensed funeral operator [1] [2]. A burial or cremation may take place once the examining physician and the civil registry have confirmed that no autopsy is required and issued the burial permit [1].
  • Burial and cremation rules: Traditional inhumation or cremation is arranged with the municipal cemetery administration or crematorium after at least 48 hours have elapsed from the time of death (unless an autopsy has already been completed) [1]. For cremation, verify that the medical report explicitly clears cremation and that no objection exists.
  • International repatriation and document legalisation: If your family member's mortal remains or ashes are to be transported outside Slovakia, the funeral director obtains a laissez-passer for a corpse (pas pre mŕtvolu) from the Regional Public Health Authority (Regionálny úrad verejného zdravotníctva), requiring hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffins for body transport [1]. For documents used abroad, EU Member States accept the Slovak death certificate with a multilingual standard form under Regulation (EU) 2016/1191, whereas non-EU jurisdictions require an Apostille from the competent regional authority or Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs, or consular legalisation [1].

steps.title: Notify Authorities and Claim Funeral and Survivor Benefits
steps.html:
• State funeral allowance (Príspevok na pohreb): An adult natural person who arranged the funeral in Slovakia may claim the statutory one-off funeral allowance through the Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs and Family of the Slovak Republic (Ministerstvo práce, sociálnych vecí a rodiny Slovenskej republiky) via the local Office of Labour, Social Affairs and Family (Úrad práce, sociálnych vecí a rodiny - ÚPSVaR) according to the deceased's last permanent or temporary residence [2] [5]. Both the applicant and the deceased must have had permanent or temporary residence in Slovakia, and the claim must be filed within one year of the date of burial using the funeral home confirmation and death certificate [2].
  • Survivor pensions (Pozostalostné dôchodky): Notify the Social Insurance Agency (Sociálna poisťovňa) to terminate the deceased's old-age or disability pension and apply for a widow's or widower's pension (vdovský alebo vdovecký dôchodok) or orphan's pension (sirotský dôchodok) [3]. Applications can be submitted at any branch of the Social Insurance Agency or electronically via the Central Public Administration Portal [3] [4].
  • Health insurance, banks, tax, and utilities: The civil registry notifies the Health Care Surveillance Authority, which updates the deceased's health insurer, though any physical health card and borrowed medical equipment should be returned [1]. Present the death certificate to Slovak banks so they can freeze sole accounts pending succession, cancel standing orders where permitted, and review any joint or beneficiary-designated products, and notify utilities, telecommunications providers, and the local municipal tax office (for real estate tax and waste fees) [4].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Notarial Succession Proceedings (*Dedičské konanie*)
steps.html:
• Automatic court initiation and notary appointment: In Slovakia, heirs do not need to file a petition to open probate. As soon as the registry office registers the death, it automatically notifies the competent district court (okresný súd) for the deceased's last permanent residence [1] [6]. The court opens succession proceedings ex officio and assigns a notary public (notár) registered with the Notarial Chamber of the Slovak Republic (Notárska komora Slovenskej republiky) to act as court commissioner (súdny komisár) according to a strict statutory court rotation schedule [6].
  • Preliminary inquiry and register of wills: The appointed notary contacts the person who arranged the funeral to conduct a preliminary investigation (predbežné vyšetrenie), identify statutory and testamentary heirs, query the Notarial Central Register of Wills (Notársky centrálny register závetov), and compile an inventory of assets and liabilities (bank balances, real estate in the cadastre, vehicles, and debts) [6].
  • Succession resolution, tax rules, and cross-border estates: Following the succession hearing, the notary issues an official Certificate of Inheritance or Court Resolution (uznesenie o dedičstve), which serves as the legal title to unfreeze bank accounts and update the real estate cadastre [6]. Slovakia abolished inheritance tax in 2004, so heirs do not pay inheritance tax on the estate, though statutory notarial fees apply based on the net value of the estate [6]. If assets or heirs are located across multiple EU countries, the notary applies EU Succession Regulation (EU) No 650/2012 and can issue a European Certificate of Succession (Európske osvedčenie o dedičstve) [6].
