title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ethiopia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ethiopia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Ethiopia: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Ethiopia. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order to handle medical certification, civil registration, funeral or international repatriation arrangements, social security and financial notifications, and succession under Ethiopian law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or health facility deaths: When your family member dies in a public referral hospital, health centre, or private clinic accredited by the Ministry of Health of Ethiopia, the attending physician completes the official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death and the health facility issues a formal Death Notification Slip [1][5]. Under Ethiopia's Registration of Vital Events and National Identity Card Proclamation (Proclamation No. 760/2012, as amended by Proclamation No. 1049/2017), health institutions are legally required to transmit death notifications to the local civil registration office [1][5].
  • Deaths at home or in the community: If a natural death occurs at home, the family or household head must obtain a supporting verification letter from the local Kebele (ward) administration or community health extension worker, along with witness statements from neighbours or the local traditional burial association (Iddir) confirming the date and place of death [1].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or medico-legal deaths: If the death is sudden, unnatural, or under investigation, the federal or regional police must be notified immediately before the body is moved [4][5]. The police refer the remains to a designated forensic pathology hospital (such as Menelik II Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Addis Ababa) for an autopsy, after which a medico-legal death report and burial release clearance are issued [4][5].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Civil Registry
steps.html:
• Issuing authority and statutory deadline: Deaths in Ethiopia must be registered with the lowest administrative level of the vital events registration office (Kebele or Woreda Vital Events Registration Office) where the death occurred or where the deceased resided [1]. In the capital, registration is administered by the Addis Ababa Civil Registration and Residency Service Agency (AACRRSA) through its sub-city and Woreda branch offices [1]. Under Proclamation No. 760/2012, a death must be declared within 30 days of occurrence [1].
  • Required documents for registration: The informant (surviving spouse, adult relative, or cohabitant) must present the hospital Medical Notification of Death (or Kebele and witness verification for a home death), the deceased's Kebele identity card, National Digital ID (Fayda), or passport, and the informant's valid identity document [1][2].
  • Obtaining the official Death Certificate: Upon registration, the civil status officer records the event in the civil register, cancels the deceased's local residency ID, and issues the official bilingual or Amharic/regional-language Death Certificate [1]. You can also track and request electronic civil and administrative verifications through the Ethiopian Government Electronic Services Portal (eServices) [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local burial or cremation: Municipal cemeteries and religious burial grounds across Ethiopia require the hospital death notification or Kebele burial permit before interment can proceed [1][5]. Many families also coordinate practical funeral arrangements and mourning support through their community mutual-aid society (Iddir) alongside licensed municipal or private funeral transport providers [1].
  • International repatriation of remains: If your family member's remains are to be repatriated abroad, a licensed funeral director and the family must obtain an official Death Certificate, an embalming and anatomical preparation certificate from an authorised hospital mortuary (such as Menelik II Hospital or St. Paul's Hospital Millennium Medical College), a non-contagious disease clearance from the Ministry of Health of Ethiopia, a hermetically sealed coffin certificate, and air cargo clearance through Ethiopian Airlines Cargo and customs authorities at Bole International Airport [1][2][5].
  • Document authentication (non-Apostille country): Because Ethiopia is not a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, Ethiopian Death Certificates and succession rulings intended for use abroad must follow a multi-step legalisation chain: first, verification by the regional vital events bureau or Addis Ababa Civil Registration and Residency Service Agency (AACRRSA); second, authentication by the Document Authentication and Registration Service (DARS) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs via the Ethiopian Government Electronic Services Portal (eServices); and third, consular legalisation by the embassy of the destination country in Addis Ababa [1][2].

steps.title: Notify Social Security, Pension, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Public-sector survivor pensions: If the deceased was a civil servant, public enterprise worker, military member, or government pensioner, survivors should file a claim with the Public Employees Social Security Administration (PSSSA) under the Public Servants' Pension Proclamation No. 1267/2022 [3]. Eligible survivors (widow or widower, minor children under 18 or under 21 if in full-time education, and dependent parents) must submit the official Death Certificate, pension ID book, marriage or birth certificates, and a court-issued certificate of heirship [3].
  • Private-sector social security claims: If your family member worked for a formal private employer covered by the Private Organizations Employees' Pension Proclamation No. 1268/2022, survivor pension and lump-sum claims are submitted to the Private Organizations Employees' Social Security Administration (POESSA) using the same civil and judicial proof of survivorship [3][4].
  • Banking, insurance, and tax closure: Notify commercial banks (such as the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia or private banks) with the Death Certificate to freeze sole accounts and prevent unauthorized withdrawals [4]. Under Ethiopian banking practice, funds in a deceased person's account are only released upon presentation of a final court succession order [4]. If the deceased operated a registered business or held a Tax Identification Number (TIN), notify the Ministry of Revenues or regional revenue bureau to settle final tax obligations [2][4].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Succession (Probate)
steps.html:
• Succession under the Ethiopian Civil Code: Estate administration is governed by Book II, Title V of the 1960 Ethiopian Civil Code and overseen by the federal or regional courts, with public legal guidance published by the Ministry of Justice of Ethiopia [4]. Ethiopian law recognises three distinct forms of wills: a Public Will (read and signed before a court registrar or notary and four or two witnesses), a Holographic Will (wholly handwritten, dated, and signed by the testator), and an Oral Will (strictly limited to imminent danger of death and restricted in scope) [4].
  • Obtaining a Judicial Certificate of Heirship: Whether the deceased died testate (with a will) or intestate (without a will), heirs or legatees must petition the Federal First Instance Court (or equivalent regional court) for a Certificate of Heirship (Ye-werashnet Maregaga'cha) and appointment of a liquidator [4]. The court publishes a notice summoning potential claimants or creditors; once the statutory notice period expires without objection, the court issues the Certificate of Heirship [4].
  • No separate inheritance tax and cross-border coordination: Ethiopia does not levy a standalone inheritance tax, though transfer fees and stamp duties apply when re-registering immovable property (urban land lease titles) or vehicles before the Document Authentication and Registration Service (DARS) and municipal land administration offices [2][4]. Heirs living abroad can appoint a representative in Ethiopia through a Special Power of Attorney legalised at an Ethiopian Embassy and registered via the Ethiopian Government Electronic Services Portal (eServices) [2][4].

closingQuestion: To help us tailor this checklist to your family member's situation, in which city or region of Ethiopia did the death occur, was the deceased an Ethiopian citizen or foreign national, and did they leave a written will?

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Ethiopia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Ethiopia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Ethiopia: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We recognise that supporting your family member through an advanced or life-limiting illness in Ethiopia requires clear coordination across healthcare providers, notarial offices, and social security institutions. Below, we set out the five key medical, legal, and administrative steps to complete in order while your family member still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Support, and Health Insurance
steps.html:
• Public hospital palliative care units: Under the National Palliative Care Strategic Plan (2025-2029) issued by the Ministry of Health of Ethiopia, multidisciplinary palliative care, pain relief (including oral liquid morphine), and symptom management are integrated across tertiary referral hospitals (such as Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital and St. Paul's Hospital Millennium Medical College in Addis Ababa, as well as regional university teaching hospitals) down to primary health centres [1]. Ask your family member's specialist for a formal referral to the hospital's pain and palliative care clinic [1].
  • Home-based nursing and hospice support: In Addis Ababa and major regional cities, hospital palliative teams coordinate with community health extension workers and specialist non-profit providers (such as Hospice Ethiopia) to deliver home nursing visits, wound care, and family caregiver training [1].
  • Community-Based Health Insurance (CBHI) and coverage: If your family member is enrolled in Ethiopia's Community-Based Health Insurance (CBHI) scheme - overseen by the Ethiopian Health Insurance Service and highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO) - verify that household membership renewals are up to date at the Woreda CBHI office so inpatient admissions, diagnostics, and essential medicines at public health centres and referral hospitals remain covered [1][5]. Formal-sector employees with private health insurance should submit specialist medical reports to pre-authorise chronic or home-care benefits [1][5].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Preferences and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Written treatment preferences: Ethiopian law does not yet codify a separate statutory living-will instrument, so medical decision-making is governed by patient autonomy and informed-consent rules under Ethiopia's Food, Medicine and Health Care Administration and Control regulations and the clinical protocols of the Ministry of Health of Ethiopia [1]. While your family member has full capacity, they should sign a written statement of care preferences specifying their wishes on intensive-care escalation, mechanical ventilation, artificial feeding, and comfort-focused care [1].
  • Designating a family medical representative: When an adult patient becomes unable to communicate, Ethiopian hospitals consult the designated family representative or next of kin listed in the clinical chart [1]. Your family member should formally record the name, telephone number, and National ID (Fayda) or Kebele ID details of their primary healthcare spokesperson in their hospital medical record and share signed copies with the treating physician [1][2].

steps.title: Execute Notarial Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• Formal Power of Attorney (Wukilna) via DARS: Under the Ethiopian Civil Code rules on agency, any Power of Attorney authorising an agent to manage bank accounts, administer or lease real property, represent the principal before tax or pension offices, or conduct legal proceedings must be executed in writing and authenticated before a notary [2][4]. In federal cities (Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa), powers of attorney are registered through the Document Authentication and Registration Service (DARS), with online appointment booking and document upload available via the Ethiopian Government Electronic Services Portal (eServices) [2].
  • Capacity verification and hospital/home attestation: A Power of Attorney (Wukilna) can only be executed while the principal possesses full mental capacity [2][4]. If your family member is physically frail or hospitalised, check with DARS or the regional Justice Bureau notary office regarding mobile or bedside authentication procedures, and obtain a contemporaneous medical certificate from the attending specialist confirming full mental alertness on the date of signing [1][2].
  • Ethiopian capacity rules and judicial interdiction: Under the Ethiopian Civil Code, a standard agency mandate is subject to revocation or termination if the principal becomes legally interdicted due to severe mental incapacity, at which point a court-appointed tutor/guardian is required [4]. In addition, commercial banks in Ethiopia require an explicit banking clause within the DARS-authenticated Power of Attorney specifying account operations, so ensure the text expressly names the relevant bank and permitted transactions [2][4].

steps.title: Activate Disability Pensions, Medical Board Assessments, and Caregiver Leave
steps.html:
• Public-sector invalidity pension claims: If your family member is a public servant or public enterprise employee covered by the Public Employees Social Security Administration (PSSSA) under Proclamation No. 1267/2022, a worker who is certified by an authorised medical board as unfit for any remunerated service due to permanent illness or disability is entitled to an invalidity pension (or invalidity gratuity if service was less than 10 years) [3]. Request a formal Medical Board referral from the treating tertiary hospital early [1][3].
  • Private-sector social security benefits: Employees of private organisations covered by Proclamation No. 1268/2022 can similarly apply to the Private Organizations Employees' Social Security Administration (POESSA) for invalidity pension benefits once a recognised Hospital Medical Board issues its permanent incapacity certificate [1][3].
  • Employment leave and caregiver arrangements: Under Ethiopia's Labour Proclamation No. 1156/2019 and Federal Civil Servants Proclamation, employees are entitled to statutory paid and partial-pay sick leave upon presenting valid medical certificates [1][3]. Family caregivers employed in the formal sector can request paid family-events leave, annual leave, or unpaid compassionate leave arrangements with their employer [3].

steps.title: Review the Will, Beneficiary Records, and Property Documentation
steps.html:
• Drafting a compliant Will under the Ethiopian Civil Code: As detailed in official guidance from the Ministry of Justice of Ethiopia, the Ethiopian Civil Code imposes strict formal requirements on wills [4]. Your family member should execute either a Public Will - read aloud and signed in the presence of a notary (such as DARS) or court registrar and four witnesses (or two witnesses if the registrar/notary officiates) - or a Holographic Will, which must be written entirely by the testator's own hand, expressly state that it is a will, and bear the exact date and signature on every page [2][4]. Lodging a Public Will with DARS significantly reduces the risk of later authenticity disputes [2][4].
  • Updating social security and civil registry files: Ensure that the marital status and birth certificates of all children and dependents are properly registered with the Addis Ababa Civil Registration and Residency Service Agency (AACRRSA) or regional vital events office, and that family dependency records filed with the Public Employees Social Security Administration (PSSSA) or POESSA match those civil certificates exactly [3][4].
  • Organising property titles and cross-border mandates: Gather urban land-holding certificates (Karta), vehicle ownership booklets (Libre), tax clearance records, and spousal consent documentation (since property acquired during marriage is presumed common property under the Revised Family Code) [2][4]. If family members reside outside Ethiopia, they can execute powers of attorney at an Ethiopian Embassy abroad and authenticate them through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ethiopian Government Electronic Services Portal (eServices) [2].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Gambia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Gambia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Gambia: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in The Gambia. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order to handle medical certification, civil registration, burial or international repatriation, social security and financial notifications, and estate administration under Gambian law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or medical facility deaths: When your family member dies in a public tertiary facility such as the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) in Banjul, a regional district hospital, or a licensed private clinic overseen by the Ministry of Health of The Gambia, the attending medical practitioner examines the deceased and issues the official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death [1][5]. You will need to provide the deceased's Gambian National Identity Card, voter card, or passport so clinical records accurately match civil registration entries [1][5].
  • Deaths at home or in rural communities: If a natural death occurs at home, the family must obtain a written attestation from the local village head (Alkalo) or ward councillor confirming the identity of the deceased and the date and place of death, and report the event to the nearest public health centre under the Ministry of Health of The Gambia for medical verification [1][2].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or medico-legal deaths: If the death is sudden, unnatural, or occurs without prior medical attendance, it must be reported immediately to the Gambia Police Force [1][3]. The police refer the case to the Coroner under The Judiciary of The Gambia and arrange transfer of the remains to the pathology mortuary at the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) for a post-mortem examination before a Coroner's burial or release order is issued [3][5].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Births and Deaths Registry
steps.html:
• Issuing authority and statutory timeframe: Under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act of The Gambia, all deaths must be registered with the Office of the Registrar of Births and Deaths operating under the Ministry of Health of The Gambia (with headquarters in Banjul and regional public health registration offices in Kanifing, Brikama, Mansakonko, Kerewan, Janjanbureh, and Basse) [1]. Statutory registration should be completed promptly - within 14 to 30 days of death - so the official certificate is available for benefits and estate administration [1][2].
  • Required documentation: A qualified informant (surviving spouse, adult child, next of kin, or person present at the death) must present the hospital Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or the Alkalo attestation and health-centre clearance for community deaths), the deceased's National ID card or passport, and the informant's own valid identification [1][2].
  • Obtaining the official Death Certificate: Upon recording the entry in the civil register, the Registrar of Births and Deaths issues the official Death Certificate [1]. It is advisable to order several certified copies at the time of registration, as pension administrators, banks, and the Probate Registry each require certified originals [1][2][3].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local burial or cremation: Municipal councils (such as Banjul City Council, Kanifing Municipal Council, and Brikama Area Council) and local community or religious cemetery committees require the hospital death notification, Coroner's order, or official Death Certificate and Burial Permit issued under the Ministry of Health of The Gambia before interment can proceed [1][5].
  • International repatriation of remains: If your family member was a foreign citizen or if the remains are to be repatriated abroad, a licensed funeral director in coordination with the mortuary at the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) must obtain the official Death Certificate, an embalming certificate, a non-infectious disease clearance from the Public Health Directorate of the Ministry of Health of The Gambia, a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin certificate, a police clearance, and customs export clearance at Banjul International Airport [1][5].
  • Consular legalisation (non-Apostille country): Because The Gambia is not a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, Gambian Death Certificates and court orders that must be used in another country require consular legalisation: first, authentication by the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Gambians Abroad in Banjul; and second, legalisation by the diplomatic mission or consulate of the destination country [3][4].

steps.title: Notify Social Security, Pension, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Social Security and Housing Finance Corporation (SSHFC) survivor claims: If the deceased contributed to the National Provident Fund (NPF), the Federated Pension Scheme (FPS), or the Industrial Injuries Compensation Fund, survivors should file a death benefit claim with the Social Security and Housing Finance Corporation (SSHFC) [2]. Claimants must submit the official Death Certificate (or verified Alkalo and medical certificate where applicable), the deceased's SSHFC social security membership card, national ID cards or birth certificates of nominated beneficiaries, and passport-sized photographs [2].
  • Civil service pensions and Gambia Revenue Authority: If the deceased was a central government civil servant or uniformed officer, notify the Personnel Management Office (PMO) and the Directorate of National Treasury to process statutory death gratuities and survivor pensions [2][3]. If the deceased held a Tax Identification Number (TIN) or operated a business, notify the Gambia Revenue Authority (GRA) to close tax accounts [3][4].
  • Commercial banks and insurers: Present the certified Death Certificate to all Gambian commercial banks where the deceased held accounts so sole accounts are frozen pending formal probate or administration authority [2][3].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Succession (Probate)
steps.html:
• High Court Probate vs. Letters of Administration: Estate succession in The Gambia is overseen by the Probate Registry of the High Court under The Judiciary of The Gambia [3]. If the deceased left a valid written Will under the Wills Act, the named executor applies to the High Court for a Grant of Probate [3]. If the deceased died intestate (without a will), the surviving family applies for Letters of Administration, or the estate may be administered through the Curator of Intestate Estates under the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia (pursuant to the Intestate Estates Act) [3][4].
  • Dual legal system (common law vs. Sharia/customary rules): Under the Laws of The Gambia, testate estates and non-Muslim intestate estates follow English-derived common law and statutory rules, whereas the intestate estates of deceased Muslims are distributed in accordance with Islamic inheritance law (Mirath) administered by the Cadi Court (Qadi Court) within The Judiciary of The Gambia, which issues the formal distribution certificate (Farid) [3][4].
  • Cross-border estates and foreign grants: The Gambia does not impose a separate inheritance tax, though court probate fees and property transfer duties apply when re-registering real property at the Deeds Registry under the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia [3][4]. Where a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration was issued in a Commonwealth or foreign country, it can be resealed by the High Court of The Gambia under the Probates (Re-sealing) Act, and heirs residing abroad may act through a consular-authenticated Power of Attorney [3][4].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Gambia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Gambia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Gambia: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We recognise that supporting your family member through an advanced or life-limiting diagnosis in The Gambia requires timely coordination across medical teams, legal registries, and social security offices. Below, we set out the five key medical, legal, and administrative steps to take in order while your family member still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Tertiary and regional medical care: Clinical management, pain relief, and specialist referrals for serious chronic or life-limiting conditions in The Gambia are coordinated through the country's main tertiary facility, the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) in Banjul, alongside regional referral hospitals (such as Kanifing General Hospital, Brikama District Hospital, and Bansang Hospital) operating under the Ministry of Health of The Gambia [1][5]. Ask the attending consultant at the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) for a written symptom-management and pain-control plan, including outpatient medication prescriptions and community clinic follow-up [1][5].
  • Home care and community clinical support: Coordinate with the hospital's medical social work unit, community health nurses under the Ministry of Health of The Gambia, or accredited private and faith-based clinics in the Greater Banjul Area to arrange home nursing visits, wound care, and caregiver guidance [1][5].
  • National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and private coverage: Check that your family member's National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) registration (linked with their Gambian biometric national ID card) or private corporate health insurance policy is active so hospital admissions, laboratory diagnostics, and covered medications at public facilities are billed properly [1][5].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Preferences and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Written statement of medical preferences: The Gambia does not have a standalone statute codifying living wills, so treatment consent and refusal are governed by common-law principles of bodily autonomy and patient-charter guidelines overseen by the Ministry of Health of The Gambia [1][5]. While your family member has full capacity, they should sign and date a written statement setting out their preferences regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intensive-care ventilation, artificial nutrition, and preferred place of care [1][5].
  • Designating a next-of-kin healthcare representative: In clinical practice at the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) and regional hospitals, doctors consult the designated next of kin or family spokesperson listed in the admission file if the patient can no longer communicate [5]. Your family member should explicitly record the full name, telephone number, and national ID details of their primary medical representative in their hospital chart and give signed copies to both the representative and the treating physician [1][5].

steps.title: Execute Financial Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• Formal Power of Attorney and Deeds Registry registration: Under Gambian common law and the Registration of Deeds Act, a Power of Attorney authorising an agent (attorney-in-fact) to manage bank accounts, lease or convey real property, or represent the principal before administrative agencies must be executed as a formal deed (signed and sealed in the presence of two witnesses and a Notary Public or Commissioner for Oaths) and registered with the Deeds Registry under the Registrar General's Department at the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia [4].
  • Capacity rules under Gambian law: Because Gambian law follows traditional common-law agency rules rather than a statutory lasting power of attorney regime, a standard Power of Attorney is valid only while the principal retains mental capacity [3][4]. If the principal later loses mental capacity, the mandate lapses and the family must petition the High Court under The Judiciary of The Gambia for a formal receivership or guardianship order to manage property [3][4].
  • Direct commercial bank account mandates: Gambian commercial banks enforce strict verification checks on third-party Powers of Attorney. While your family member retains full capacity, arrange to complete the bank's own third-party signatory mandate form directly at the branch (or request a home/hospital verification visit from the branch manager) alongside the registered Power of Attorney [4].

steps.title: Activate Invalidity Benefits, Pension Claims, and Caregiver Leave
steps.html:
• Invalidity benefits via the SSHFC: If your family member is a member of the National Provident Fund (NPF) or the Federated Pension Scheme (FPS) administered by the Social Security and Housing Finance Corporation (SSHFC), they may claim an Invalidity Benefit or medical early retirement pension if certified by an approved Medical Board as permanently incapable of work due to physical or mental illness [2]. Early submission of the specialist medical report from the Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH) helps expedite the Medical Board assessment [2][5].
  • Civil service ill-health retirement: Public servants employed by the Government of The Gambia who become permanently unfit for service due to severe illness can apply through their ministry and the Personnel Management Office for medical boarding under the Pensions Act, following certification by a Government Medical Board convened through the Ministry of Health of The Gambia [1][2].
  • Workplace sick leave and caregiver leave: Under The Gambia's Labour Act, formal employees are entitled to statutory paid sick leave upon presenting medical certificates, and family caregivers can request annual leave, compassionate leave, or flexible working arrangements through their employer's human resources department [2].

steps.title: Organise the Will, Beneficiary Nominations, and Property Records
steps.html:
• Updating SSHFC nominee records: Payouts from the Social Security and Housing Finance Corporation (SSHFC) rely heavily on the official Nomination Form filed by the member during their lifetime [2]. While your family member has full capacity, they should verify and update their designated nominees with the SSHFC and ensure that all nominees hold valid birth certificates or national ID cards issued through the Births and Deaths Registry or Immigration Department [1][2].
  • Executing a valid Will and dual-system rules: Under the Wills Act of The Gambia, a written Will must be signed by the testator in the simultaneous presence of at least two independent attesting witnesses who are not beneficiaries [3][4]. Note that under the Laws of The Gambia, the estate of a person subject to Islamic personal law is governed by Sharia inheritance rules (Mirath) administered by the Cadi Court under The Judiciary of The Gambia (where testamentary bequests, Wasiyyah, are generally limited to one-third of the net estate to non-heirs unless statutory heirs consent) [3][4].
  • Consolidating property titles and cross-border documents: Gather land title deeds or state lease documents registered at the Deeds Registry of the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia, marriage certificates, and bank records in one secure file [4]. Because The Gambia is not a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, powers of attorney or property documents executed abroad must be legalised through a Gambian Embassy or High Commission and authenticated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Justice of The Gambia [3][4].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ghana: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ghana: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Ghana: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Ghana. Navigating medical certification, civil registration, funeral permits, survivor claims, and succession procedures in Ghana involves several statutory authorities and strict documentation requirements. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order so that your family can manage each stage methodically.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Cause of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or health-facility deaths: When a person dies in a hospital, clinic, or accredited health facility overseen by the Ministry of Health of Ghana and the Ghana Health Service, the attending medical practitioner examines the body and issues an official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death [3]. You should verify that your family member's full legal name, age, national identification details, and exact date and place of death match their official identity records before leaving the facility [3].
  • Deaths at home or outside a medical facility: If your family member died at home after a known illness under recent medical care, the attending doctor may still issue the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death after examining the remains, or the body must be conveyed to a public hospital mortuary for formal medical verification [1] [3].
  • Unexpected, sudden, or unnatural deaths: Under the Coroners Act, 1960 (Act 18) and the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 2020 (Act 1027), any sudden, accidental, unexplained, or non-natural death must be reported immediately to the Ghana Police Service [1] [4]. Police officers refer the matter to the district coroner (typically the District Magistrate within the Judicial Service of Ghana), who orders a post-mortem examination by a pathologist and issues a Coroner's Certificate or Burial Order before civil registration and burial can proceed [1] [4].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Births and Deaths Registry
steps.html:
• Mandatory civil registration and statutory timelines: Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 2020 (Act 1027), all deaths occurring in Ghana must be registered with the Births and Deaths Registry in the registration district where the death occurred [1]. Standard registration should be completed before burial and within the statutory registration period (within 14 days of death for standard timely registration, after which late registration procedures and additional statutory fees apply) [1].
  • Who may register and required documents: A surviving spouse, adult relative, household head, or person present at the death acts as the informant at the district office of the Births and Deaths Registry or via the integrated public portal on Ghana.gov [1]. The informant must present the original Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or Coroner's Certificate), the deceased's Ghana Card (National Identification Card) or passport, and the informant's own valid photo identification [1].
  • Burial Permit and certified Death Certificate: Upon recording the entry in the register of deaths, the District Registrar of the Births and Deaths Registry issues a Burial Permit (required to release the body for interment or cremation) and an official Death Certificate [1]. It is advisable to request several certified extracts or copies of the Death Certificate, as banks, insurers, pension authorities, and probate courts require original or certified copies [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Licensed mortuary and funeral arrangements: You should engage a licensed funeral home or hospital mortuary regulated under the Mortuaries and Funeral Facilities Act, 1998 (Act 563) and the Health Institutions and Facilities Act, 2011 (Act 829) under the Ministry of Health of Ghana [3]. No cemetery or crematorium may conduct a burial or cremation without the official Burial Permit issued by the Births and Deaths Registry and municipal environmental health clearance from the local Metropolitan, Municipal, or District Assembly (MMDA) [1] [3].
  • International repatriation of human remains or ashes: If your family member's remains or cremated ashes are to be repatriated out of Ghana, the funeral director must obtain an embalming certificate, a non-infectious disease clearance certificate from the Port Health Unit of the Ministry of Health of Ghana, a coroner's or police clearance for exportation of remains, a zinc-lined hermetically sealed coffin certificate (for body transport), and a consular mortuary laissez-passer from the destination country's embassy or high commission in Accra [1] [3].
  • Document legalization for foreign use: Because Ghana is not currently a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, a Ghanaian Death Certificate or court order intended for use in a foreign jurisdiction must undergo full diplomatic legalization - starting with authentication by the Judicial Service of Ghana or Notary Public and the Legal and Consular Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration, followed by consular legalization at the relevant foreign embassy [1] [4].

steps.title: Notify Social Security, Pension, Tax, Banking, and Identity Authorities
steps.html:
• Claiming SSNIT Survivors Lump Sum Benefits: If your family member contributed to the First Tier basic national social security scheme or was receiving a retirement pension, nominated dependents or legal beneficiaries should report the death to the nearest branch of the Social Security and National Insurance Trust [2]. Under the National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), when a member dies before retirement (having met minimum contribution requirements, such as 12 months within the preceding 36 months) or dies before age 75 while on pension, the Social Security and National Insurance Trust pays a Survivors Lump Sum Benefit to nominated dependents or court-recognized beneficiaries [2]. Applicants must submit the official Death Certificate, Medical Certificate of Cause of Death, valid Ghana Cards of beneficiaries, birth certificates for minor children, and employer clearance if the deceased died in active service [2].
  • Tier 2 and Tier 3 occupational pension funds: In addition to First Tier claims with the Social Security and National Insurance Trust, families should contact the deceased's corporate trustee licensed by the National Pensions Regulatory Authority (NPRA) to claim any Second Tier mandatory occupational lump sum and Third Tier provident fund balances [2].
  • Tax, identity cards, and banking notifications: You should notify the National Identification Authority (NIA) and the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) to deactivate the deceased's Ghana Card and health insurance membership, and notify commercial banks to freeze sole accounts pending probate or Letters of Administration [1] [5]. The estate representative must also notify the Ghana Revenue Authority to settle any outstanding personal income tax or business tax liabilities accrued up to the date of death [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Probate, or Intestate Succession
steps.html:
• Testate succession (Application for Probate): If your family member left a valid written will executed in accordance with the Wills Act, 1971 (Act 360), the named executors must apply to the Probate and Administration Division of the High Court (or the District/Circuit Court if the estate value falls within lower statutory thresholds) within the Judicial Service of Ghana [4]. Once the will is read and proved in court, the court issues a formal Grant of Probate authorizing the executors to collect assets, settle debts, and sign Vesting Assents transferring property to beneficiaries [4].
  • Intestate succession (Letters of Administration under PNDCL 111): If your family member died without a valid will, estate distribution is governed by the Intestate Succession Law, 1985 (PNDCL 111), which protects the surviving spouse and children by allocating the household chattels, primary residence, and the majority statutory share of the residue to the nuclear family before customary family shares [4]. At least two applicants (typically representing the surviving spouse/children and the customary family) must petition the court within the Judicial Service of Ghana for Letters of Administration, preceded by a mandatory court notice posted for at least 21 days [2] [4].
  • Tax filings and cross-border estate coordination: While Ghana does not levy a separate general inheritance tax on bequests to heirs, the Ghana Revenue Authority requires tax clearance for property transfers, capital realizations, or business closures, and stamp duty/registration fees apply at the Lands Commission when registering a Vesting Assent [4] [5]. If heirs reside outside Ghana or assets are held across multiple countries, foreign heirs may appoint a representative in Ghana via a notarized and consulate-legalized Power of Attorney, or apply to the High Court of Ghana to reseal a foreign grant of probate [4].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Ghana: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Ghana: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Ghana: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Ghana is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, taking timely medical, legal, and financial steps while they retain full mental and legal decision-making capacity helps protect their comfort, autonomy, and property. Below, we outline the five essential official and practical steps to coordinate care, medical directives, powers of attorney, social security benefits, and estate documentation in Ghana.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Specialist palliative and pain-management clinics: You can request a referral from your family member's treating specialist to dedicated multidisciplinary palliative care units operating within public teaching hospitals overseen by the Ministry of Health of Ghana and the Ghana Health Service, including the Palliative Care Units at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra, Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital in Kumasi, and the Tetteh Quarshie Memorial Hospital [1] [5]. These teams manage complex pain control (including regulated oral morphine prescriptions), symptom relief, and domiciliary nursing visits [1] [5].
  • National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) coverage: You should verify that your family member's membership with the National Health Insurance Authority is active so that covered inpatient admissions, outpatient consultations, diagnostic investigations, and essential medicines on the NHIS Medicines List are billed directly at accredited public and private facilities [2].
  • Home care and private health insurance: If your family member holds private health insurance or an employer medical plan, contact the insurer early to confirm pre-authorization rules for home nursing care, medical equipment rental, and specialist oncology or palliative consultations [1] [2].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Preferences and Designate a Medical Proxy
steps.html:
• Patient's Charter and informed consent rights: Under the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851) - which incorporates the Ghana Health Service Patient's Charter - every patient with decision-making capacity has the statutory right to receive full clinical information, to consent to or refuse specific medical treatments, and to involve designated family representatives in care decisions [1] [4].
  • Written advance care plan and treatment directives: Although Ghana does not have a standalone Living Wills statute, your family member can sign a written Advance Care Directive while mentally competent, clearly stating their preferences regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation, mechanical ventilation, intensive care admission, pain management, and preferred place of care (hospital vs. home) [1] [4].
  • Designating a healthcare representative in clinical records: Your family member should formally name a primary and alternate healthcare representative (medical proxy) in writing, have the document witnessed and placed directly into their hospital medical file, and review these wishes with the lead clinician at the Ministry of Health of Ghana facility so the care team knows whom to consult if capacity later declines [1] [5].

steps.title: Execute Financial and Legal Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• Statutory requirements under the Powers of Attorney Act, 1998 (Act 549): While your family member retains full mental capacity, they can execute a formal Power of Attorney under the Powers of Attorney Act, 1998 (Act 549) authorizing a trusted attorney-in-fact to manage property, sign legal instruments, and handle administrative affairs [4]. Under Act 549, the instrument must be signed by the donor (or at their direction in their presence) and attested by at least one witness (or two witnesses if signed by someone else at the donor's direction) [4].
  • Notarization, stamping, and registration: To be accepted by public registries, courts, and financial institutions, the Power of Attorney should be notarized by a Notary Public, stamped for stamp duty at the Lands Commission / Ghana Revenue Authority, and registered where land or real property transactions are involved [4]. Note that under Ghanaian common-law agency rules, an ordinary Power of Attorney is suspended or ceases to operate if the donor loses mental capacity, after which family members would need to apply to the High Court within the Judicial Service of Ghana for a formal guardianship or receivership order under the Mental Health Act, 2012 (Act 846) [4].
  • Direct bank mandates and digital access: Because commercial banks in Ghana enforce strict internal verification rules, your family member should visit their bank branches in person (or request a domiciliary relationship-manager visit) to sign the bank's own third-party mandate or joint-signatory forms while fully lucid [4].

steps.title: Activate Invalidity, Critical-Illness, and Caregiver Support Benefits
steps.html:
• SSNIT Invalidity Pension: If your family member is an active worker under retirement age who has become permanently incapable of any normal gainful employment due to a severe or terminal physical or mental condition, they can apply for an Invalidity Pension from the Social Security and National Insurance Trust [3]. Under the National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), the member must have contributed for at least 12 months within the last 36 months and must be certified as permanently invalid by a recognized Medical Board following a report from an accredited medical practitioner [3].
  • Tier 2 and Tier 3 pension disability withdrawals and insurance: Approved invalidity status also entitles the member to claim lump-sum accrued balances from their Second Tier mandatory occupational pension scheme and Third Tier voluntary provident fund managed by their NPRA-licensed trustee, as well as any critical-illness or permanent-disability rider on private life insurance policies [3].
  • Employment leave and workplace protections: Under the Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), employees in Ghana are entitled to statutory paid annual leave and certified medical/sick leave, and family caregivers can negotiate compassionate leave or flexible working arrangements with their employer while supporting a seriously ill family member [4].

steps.title: Organize the Will, Beneficiary Nominations, and Property Records
steps.html:
• Executing or updating a valid Will under the Wills Act, 1971 (Act 360): Preparing a clear written will prevents the delays and potential family disputes associated with intestacy under the Intestate Succession Law, 1985 (PNDCL 111) [4]. Under the Wills Act, 1971 (Act 360), the testator must be at least 18 years old and of sound mind, and must sign the will in the simultaneous presence of at least two witnesses (neither of whom may be a beneficiary or spouse of a beneficiary under the will) [4].
  • Safekeeping at the High Court Registry: Once executed, the original will can be sealed and deposited for official safekeeping at the Probate Registry of the High Court within the Judicial Service of Ghana, ensuring it cannot be lost, altered, or suppressed [4].
  • Updating SSNIT and pension beneficiary nominations: Because First Tier Survivors Lump Sum Benefits and Tier 2/Tier 3 occupational pension funds are paid primarily according to recorded beneficiary nominations, your family member should contact the Social Security and National Insurance Trust to review and update their beneficiary nomination records and ensure all dependents' Ghana Card details and birth certificates are accurate [3].
  • Consolidating property titles and cross-border assets: Gather original Land Title Certificates, registered indentures, vehicle registration books, and bank details in a secure folder [4]. If your family member owns assets outside Ghana or has heirs living abroad, ensure any foreign Power of Attorney or separate situs will is executed and legalized through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration and the relevant foreign embassy [4].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Kenya: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Kenya: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Kenya: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Kenya. Managing medical certification, civil registration, burial or repatriation permits, social security claims, and succession proceedings in Kenya involves specific statutory forms and digital government portals. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Cause of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or medical-facility deaths (Form D1): When a death occurs in a hospital or clinical facility regulated by the Ministry of Health, the attending medical practitioner examines the remains and completes the statutory Medical Certificate of Cause of Death - Death in Hospital (Form D1) under the Births and Deaths Registration Act (Cap. 149) [1] [4]. Ensure that your family member's full legal name, national ID or passport number, age, and date and place of death match their official identity documents [1].
  • Deaths at home or outside a health facility (Form D2): If your family member died naturally at home without an attending physician, the death must be reported immediately to the local National Government Administration Officer (Area Chief or Assistant Chief) and the nearest police station so the body can be transferred to an accredited mortuary and a Death Notification (Form D2) can be issued [1] [4].
  • Sudden, accidental, or unexplained deaths (Form D3 / Police and Inquest Clearance): Under the Criminal Procedure Code and the National Coroners Service framework, any sudden, accidental, or non-natural death must be reported to the National Police Service [1] [4]. A government pathologist conducts a post-mortem examination and issues a Police/Pathologist Death Notification (Form D3) together with a post-mortem report before burial or civil registration can proceed [1] [4].

steps.title: Register the Death with Civil Registration Services
steps.html:
• Mandatory registration and statutory deadlines: Under the Births and Deaths Registration Act (Cap. 149), every death occurring in Kenya must be registered with the Department of Civil Registration Services [1] [4]. Current death registration applies within six months of the date of death; deaths reported after six months require the formal Late Death Registration procedure, supporting affidavits, and additional verification fees [1] [4].
  • Applying via eCitizen and Civil Registration offices: Upon issuance of Form D1, D2, or D3, the hospital, mortuary, or local registrar issues a Permit for Burial (Burial Permit) so funeral arrangements can proceed [1]. The next of kin then applies for the official Death Certificate through the Department of Civil Registration Services portal on eCitizen (or at the Sub-County Civil Registrar's office / Huduma Centre) by uploading the original Burial Permit, the Death Notification (Form D1, D2, or D3), a copy of the deceased's Kenya National ID Card or passport, and the applicant's National ID [1].
  • Obtaining certified copies: Once approved by the Department of Civil Registration Services, the official Death Certificate is issued [1]. It is advisable to keep multiple certified copies, as courts, banks, pension schemes, and tax authorities each require proof of death [1] [4].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Licensed funeral home and local burial or cremation: Families should coordinate transport, mortuary preservation, and interment or cremation through a licensed funeral home or county public mortuary operating under the Public Health Act (Cap. 242) overseen by the Ministry of Health [1] [4]. No cemetery or crematorium in Kenya may conduct a burial or cremation without the original Burial Permit and county public health clearance [1] [4].
  • International repatriation of human remains or ashes: If your family member's remains or cremated ashes must be repatriated abroad, the funeral director must secure an official Death Certificate from the Department of Civil Registration Services, an embalming certificate, a non-infectious disease clearance and export permit from Port Health Services under the Ministry of Health, a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin certificate (for body repatriation), police clearance, and a consular mortuary laissez-passer from the destination country's embassy or high commission in Nairobi [1] [4].
  • Document authentication and legalization: Because Kenya is not currently a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, a Kenyan Death Certificate or court grant intended for official use abroad must be authenticated by the Registrar-General / Judiciary of Kenya and legalized by the Legal and Host Country Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, followed by consular legalization at the destination country's embassy in Nairobi [1] [4].

steps.title: Notify Social Security, Health Insurance, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• National Social Security Fund (NSSF) Survivors' Benefit and Funeral Grant: If your family member was a registered contributor to the National Social Security Fund, surviving dependents (spouse, children, or dependent parents) should report the death to the nearest NSSF branch under the NSSF Act, No. 45 of 2013 [2] [4]. The National Social Security Fund provides a statutory Funeral Grant to assist with immediate burial expenses (claimed using the Burial Permit or Death Certificate, claimant ID, and funeral receipts) and a Survivors' Benefit paying out the member's accumulated Tier I and Tier II retirement credit to verified dependents [2] [4].
  • Social Health Authority (SHA) and identity records: Notify the Social Health Authority (which replaced the former NHIF under the Social Health Insurance Act, 2023) to settle any final inpatient hospital claims and deactivate the member's health insurance record [3]. The deceased's original National Identity Card is surrendered during death registration so the National Registration Bureau can update the population register [1].
  • Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) and bank notifications: Notify all commercial banks and SACCOs where the deceased held accounts so sole accounts are frozen pending succession orders [4] [5]. The legal representative must also notify the Kenya Revenue Authority via the iTax portal to file taxes accrued up to the date of death and wind up the deceased's KRA PIN once estate administration concludes [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate and Obtain a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration
steps.html:
• Filing a succession cause under the Law of Succession Act (Cap. 160): Under Section 45 of the Law of Succession Act (Cap. 160), handling or distributing a deceased person's property without court authority constitutes unlawful intermeddling [4]. All succession petitions are filed electronically through the Judiciary of Kenya e-Filing portal at the High Court Family Division or the Chief Magistrate's Court (depending on the pecuniary value of the estate) [4].
  • Testate vs. intestate procedure and Kenya Gazette notice: If your family member left a valid written or oral will, the executors petition for a Grant of Probate [4]. If they died intestate (without a will), surviving spouses and adult children have priority to petition for a Grant of Letters of Administration Intestate, accompanied by a letter from the local Area Chief listing all surviving dependents and a schedule of assets and liabilities [4]. The Judiciary of Kenya publishes a mandatory 30-day notice of the petition in the Kenya Gazette before issuing the initial grant, followed after six months (or earlier in special circumstances) by a Summons for Confirmation of Grant authorizing the distribution of assets [4].
  • Taxation and cross-border succession: Kenya does not levy an estate or inheritance tax (Estate Duty was abolished), and transmissions of property from an estate representative to a beneficiary are exempt from Capital Gains Tax and stamp duty, though registration fees and KRA tax clearance on rental or business income still apply through the Kenya Revenue Authority [4] [5]. If the deceased held a foreign grant of probate from a Commonwealth or designated country, the High Court within the Judiciary of Kenya can reseal that foreign grant under Section 77 of the Law of Succession Act so Kenyan assets can be administered [4].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Kenya: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Kenya: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Kenya: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Kenya is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, putting clear medical, legal, and financial arrangements in place while they retain full mental and legal decision-making capacity protects their dignity and prevents administrative delays. Below, we set out the five key official and practical steps to coordinate palliative care, advance medical directives, powers of attorney, disability benefits, and estate planning in Kenya.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Social Health Authority Coverage
steps.html:
• Public and specialist palliative care services: You can request a formal referral from your family member's treating specialist to hospital-based palliative care units operating in national referral and county hospitals overseen by the Ministry of Health (such as Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, and county referral palliative clinics) or accredited community hospices coordinated with the Kenya Hospices and Palliative Care Association [1] [5]. These multidisciplinary teams provide pain management (including regulated opioid analgesics), symptom control, and home-based nursing visits [1] [5].
  • Social Health Authority (SHA) and Critical Illness Fund: Under the Social Health Insurance Act, 2023, verify that your family member is registered and up to date with the Social Health Authority [1]. The Social Health Authority manages the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) and the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund (ECCIF), which cover oncology treatments, renal care, inpatient palliative admissions, and chronic symptom management at accredited public, faith-based, and private facilities [1].
  • Private medical insurance and home-care pre-authorization: If your family member has private medical insurance or an employer-sponsored medical scheme, contact the insurer's case-management desk early to pre-authorize home nursing care, oxygen or medical equipment rental, and palliative consultations [1] [5].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Directives and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Statutory patient rights under the Health Act, 2017: Under Sections 8 and 9 of the Health Act, No. 21 of 2017, every patient in Kenya has the statutory right to full informed consent, the right to refuse medical treatment (unless refusal poses a serious public health risk), and the right to designate a representative to make healthcare decisions if they become incapacitated [1] [2].
  • Executing a written Advance Medical Directive (Living Will): While your family member has full mental capacity, they can sign a written Advance Healthcare Directive specifying their wishes regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (Do Not Attempt Resuscitation orders), mechanical ventilation, artificial nutrition, pain relief, and preferred place of care [1] [2].
  • Designating a healthcare proxy in hospital records: Your family member should formally name a primary and alternate medical representative in writing, have the directive witnessed by two independent adults (and optionally attested by an Advocate of the High Court of Kenya), and provide signed copies to their treating physician at the Ministry of Health or private hospital so it is placed prominently in their medical file [1] [2].

steps.title: Execute Financial and Legal Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• General and Special Powers of Attorney: While your family member retains full legal capacity, they should instruct an Advocate of the High Court of Kenya to draft a General or Special Power of Attorney authorizing a trusted representative to manage bank accounts, pay medical bills, collect rent, and deal with property [2].
  • Stamping and compulsory registration (Land Registration Act, 2012): Under the Stamp Duty Act (Cap. 480) and the Registration of Documents Act (Cap. 285) / Land Registration Act, No. 3 of 2012, any Power of Attorney must be executed in the prescribed statutory form, attested by an advocate or Notary Public, assessed for stamp duty, and registered at the Registry of Documents or the Ardhisasa Land Registry (within 60 days of execution) to be legally valid for property or institutional transactions [2]. Note that under Kenyan law, an ordinary Power of Attorney ceases to be valid if the donor loses mental capacity; if capacity is lost, family members must petition the High Court within the Judiciary of Kenya for a formal guardianship and management order under Section 26 of the Mental Health Act (Cap. 248) [2].
  • Direct bank signing mandates: Because Kenyan commercial banks verify account mandates strictly, your family member should also sign each bank's internal third-party operating mandate or joint-signatory resolution in person (or via a domiciliary bank relationship visit) while still mobile and lucid [2].

steps.title: Activate Invalidity, Disability, and Caregiver Support Benefits
steps.html:
• NSSF Invalidity Benefit: If your family member is a contributor to the National Social Security Fund who has become permanently incapable of engaging in gainful employment due to a severe physical or mental disability or terminal condition before reaching standard retirement age, they can apply for an Invalidity Benefit under Section 38 of the NSSF Act, No. 45 of 2013 [2] [3]. The claim requires a formal medical assessment by a registered medical practitioner and certification by the NSSF medical board [3].
  • Registration with the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD): If the illness causes long-term physical, sensory, or functional impairment, your family member can undergo a medical assessment at a county hospital (via the eCitizen NCPWD portal) to register with the National Council for Persons with Disabilities [4]. An NCPWD disability certificate entitles a Kenyan resident to an income-tax exemption (up to KES 150,000 per month on employment or pension income under the Persons with Disabilities Act and Kenya Revenue Authority rules) as well as access to assistive devices and social protection programs [2] [4].
  • Occupational pension disability rules and employment leave: Check any private or public service occupational pension scheme regulated by the Retirement Benefits Authority (RBA) for ill-health early retirement lump-sum options, as well as critical-illness riders on life policies [2] [3]. Under the Employment Act, 2007, employees are entitled to statutory paid sick leave, and working family caregivers can request compassionate leave or flexible scheduling from their employers [2].

steps.title: Review the Will, Beneficiary Nominations, and Property Documents
steps.html:
• Drafting or updating a valid Will under the Law of Succession Act (Cap. 160): Executing a clear written will avoids the lengthy court disputes often associated with intestate estates [2]. Under Section 11 of the Law of Succession Act (Cap. 160), a written will is valid only if the testator possesses sound disposing mind, signs or affixes their mark to the document, and has their signature attested by at least two competent independent witnesses who sign in the presence of the testator [2]. The executed will can be kept in safe custody with the testator's advocate, bank, or the High Court Registry within the Judiciary of Kenya [2].
  • Reviewing pension and insurance beneficiary nominations: Under Kenyan retirement-benefits law, nominated pension benefits and group life assurance proceeds are generally paid directly by trustees to nominated dependents outside the lengthy court probate process [2] [3]. Your family member should update their nomination forms with the National Social Security Fund, their RBA occupational pension scheme, and their SACCO so that beneficiaries and minor children's details are current [3].
  • Organizing civil records, Ardhisasa land titles, and cross-border assets: Compile original Title Deeds (and verify digital land records on the Ardhisasa platform), logbooks on the NTSA TIMS portal, share certificates (CDSC accounts), marriage certificates, and children's birth certificates [2]. If your family member holds assets outside Kenya or has heirs abroad, coordinate with an advocate to prepare a separate situs will or authenticate any cross-border Power of Attorney through a Notary Public and the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs [2].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Lesotho: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Lesotho: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Lesotho: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Lesotho. Managing medical certification, civil registration, burial or repatriation permits, survivor claims, and estate administration in the Kingdom of Lesotho involves specific statutory procedures across local authorities, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Master of the High Court. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Cause of Death
steps.html:
• Deaths in a hospital or health facility: When a person dies in a public hospital (such as Queen 'Mamohato Memorial Hospital or a district government hospital), Christian Health Association of Lesotho (CHAL) facility, or private clinic regulated under the Ministry of Health in Lesotho, the attending medical practitioner examines the body and issues an official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Medical Report) [1] [3]. Check that your family member's full legal name, Lesotho National Identity number, age, and exact date and place of death match their official identity records [1].
  • Deaths at home or in a rural village: If your family member died naturally at home in a village or urban community, the family must first report the death to the local Area Chief or Village Chief, who issues a written Chief's Notification Letter confirming the death in the community [1] [2]. The remains are transferred to a licensed mortuary and verified so a medical confirmation or mortuary record can accompany the Chief's letter [1].
  • Sudden, unnatural, or accidental deaths: Under the Inquests Proclamation and Lesotho criminal procedure laws, any sudden, accidental, or unexplained death must be reported immediately to the Lesotho Mounted Police Service (LMPS) [2]. Police authorities arrange a medico-legal post-mortem examination by a government pathologist before issuing clearance for burial and civil death registration [1] [2].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Ministry of Home Affairs (NICR)
steps.html:
• Mandatory civil registration and statutory timelines: Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1973 and the National Identity Cards Act, 2011, all deaths occurring in Lesotho must be registered with the Department of National Identity and Civil Registration (NICR) within the Ministry of Home Affairs [1] [2]. Deaths should be reported promptly at the nearest district NICR office so a burial permit and official Death Certificate can be issued [1].
  • Required documents for death registration: To obtain a Death Certificate from the Ministry of Home Affairs, the informant (a close relative or authorized family representative) must submit the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death from the doctor or hospital, the letter from the local Chief confirming the death, the deceased's original Lesotho National ID Card (or passport/birth certificate), and certified copies of the informant's own National ID Card [1].
  • Obtaining certified copies of the Death Certificate: Once the district registrar verifies the records and cancels the deceased's National ID in the national population register, the Ministry of Home Affairs issues the official Death Certificate [1]. Request several certified copies of the Death Certificate, as banks, insurers, pension funds, and the Master of the High Court require certified copies [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Engaging a licensed funeral parlour and burial clearance: Families typically engage a licensed funeral provider in Lesotho to manage mortuary care, coffin preparation, and local interment [1] [3]. For burial in an urban municipal cemetery (such as in Maseru) or a community burial ground, the family must present the official Death Certificate or burial order together with clearance from the local council or Area Chief [1] [4].
  • Cross-border and international repatriation of remains: Because many families travel or repatriate remains across the border with South Africa or further abroad, international repatriation requires an official Death Certificate from the Ministry of Home Affairs, a Medical Certificate of Cause of Death confirming a non-communicable cause of death, an embalming certificate from a licensed funeral director, an export/removal permit from the Ministry of Health port health authorities, police clearance, and consular or border clearance for entry into South Africa or the destination country [1] [3].
  • Apostille and document authentication: Lesotho is a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention [2] [4]. If a Lesotho Death Certificate, marriage certificate, or High Court order must be used in another Hague Apostille member state, it can be authenticated with an official Apostille certificate through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Relations or the High Court registrar; for non-Hague countries, standard diplomatic and consular legalization applies [2] [4].

steps.title: Notify Pension, Social Protection, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Public Officers' Defined Contribution Pension Fund and occupational schemes: If your family member was a civil servant or public officer, report the death to the Public Officers' Defined Contribution Pension Fund (or the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning pensions division) to claim the statutory death-in-service lump sum, funeral benefit, and surviving spouse's or children's pension [2] [4]. For private-sector workers or cross-border mineworkers, notify the relevant occupational provident fund, funeral policy insurer, or the Mineworkers Provident Fund / TEBA office in Lesotho [2] [4].
  • Old Age Pension and social assistance notifications: If the deceased was age 70 or older and receiving Lesotho's non-contributory Old Age Pension or social assistance grants through the Ministry of Gender, Youth and Social Development / Ministry of Finance, notify the district paymaster office with the Death Certificate so payments cease and any final accrued arrears are settled [4].
  • Revenue Services Lesotho (RSL) and banking notifications: Notify all commercial banks and mobile-money operators (such as M-Pesa and EcoCash) to freeze sole accounts pending the appointment of an estate executor [2] [5]. The estate representative must also notify Revenue Services Lesotho to file any final personal income tax or business tax returns up to the date of death and obtain tax clearance [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate before the Master of the High Court
steps.html:
• Reporting the estate under the Administration of Estates and Inheritance Act, 2024: Lesotho modernized and unified its succession law under the landmark Administration of Estates and Inheritance Act, 2024 (replacing the colonial Administration of Estates Proclamation 19 of 1935 and abolishing discriminatory customary male-primogeniture rules) [2]. Every deceased estate must be reported to the Office of the Master of the High Court (located in Maseru or via the District Administrator's office in other districts) within the Lesotho Judiciary [2].
  • Testate vs. intestate succession and equal inheritance rights: If your family member left a valid written will, the Master of the High Court registers the will and issues Letters of Executorship to the named executor [2]. If your family member died intestate (without a will), the Administration of Estates and Inheritance Act, 2024 protects the surviving spouse and guarantees equal inheritance shares for all children of the deceased regardless of gender or whether born in or out of wedlock, and the Master of the High Court issues Letters of Authority or appoints a dative executor after family consultation and statutory notice [2].
  • Estate duties, land transfers, and cross-border assets: The executor must compile a liquidation and distribution account, obtain tax clearance from Revenue Services Lesotho, and register any transfer of residential or commercial land leases with the Land Administration Authority (LAA) [2] [5]. If your family member held bank accounts, pensions, or immovable property in South Africa or another foreign country, the Lesotho Letters of Executorship must be authenticated (by Apostille) and presented to the foreign Master of the High Court for resealing or ancillary estate administration [2] [4].
