title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Palau: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Palau: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Palau: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We understand that managing an advanced or life-limiting illness for your family member in the Republic of Palau requires coordinated medical, legal, and administrative preparation. Taking structured steps while your family member retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity ensures that palliative care, healthcare consent directives, financial powers of attorney, social security disability benefits, and estate and customary property records are properly arranged. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and National Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Hospital and community supportive care: Coordinate primary and specialist medical care through Belau National Hospital in Koror and the community health centers overseen by the Ministry of Health and Human Services [1] [6]. Ask the attending physician for a comprehensive written clinical summary (Diagnosis and Treatment Plan) and arrange outpatient pain management, chronic-disease home visits, or medical equipment support through the Bureau of Public Health and Home Health services [1].
  • National Healthcare Financing Program (HealthCare Fund and MSA): Verify your family member's active enrollment in the Palau National Health Insurance (NHI) and their individual Medical Savings Account (MSA) administered by the Republic of Palau Social Security Administration under Title 41 of the Palau National Code (41 PNC) [4]. The pooled National Health Insurance account covers up to 80 to 90 percent of eligible inpatient care at Belau National Hospital and approved off-island medical referrals, while the individual Medical Savings Account can be drawn down to pay co-payments, outpatient prescriptions, and supportive care costs [4].
  • Off-island medical referral coordination: If specialized oncology or palliative procedures require referral to an accredited tertiary hospital outside Palau (such as in the Philippines, Taiwan, Guam, or Hawaii), submit the treating physician's referral request to the Medical Referral Committee at the Ministry of Health and Human Services before travel so coverage limits are pre-authorized [1] [4].

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Directives and Designate a Healthcare Proxy
steps.html:
• Informed consent and treatment preferences: Under the health and patients' rights framework administered by the Ministry of Health and Human Services (34 PNC), an adult patient with full mental capacity has the right to give or withhold informed consent to invasive surgical or life-prolonging interventions and to specify comfort-focused care goals (including Do-Not-Resuscitate or non-intubation orders) in consultation with their attending physician at Belau National Hospital [1] [6].
  • Written Advance Healthcare Directive and Medical Proxy: While your family member retains full decision-making capacity, have them execute a written Advance Healthcare Directive and Healthcare Power of Attorney naming a trusted primary adult medical representative (and an alternate) authorized to make clinical and off-island referral decisions if your family member later becomes unable to communicate [1] [3].
  • Hospital chart filing and capacity verification: Ask the attending physician at Belau National Hospital to document your family member's current mental capacity (sound mind and orientation) in the medical chart and place signed copies of the Advance Healthcare Directive and Healthcare Proxy directly in the Medical Records Office of the Ministry of Health and Human Services [1].

steps.title: Execute Financial Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates While Capacity Is Intact
steps.html:
• Durable or General Power of Attorney: Under Palauan civil and common-law principles recognized by the Palau Supreme Court (1 PNC § 303), an adult principal with full legal capacity may execute a written General or Durable Power of Attorney (POA) appointing an attorney-in-fact to manage bank accounts, business licenses, tax filings with the Ministry of Finance, and personal property [3] [5]. To ensure the instrument remains valid if the ill person later loses mental capacity, include explicit durable language (this Power of Attorney shall not be affected by the subsequent disability or incapacity of the principal) and have the signature acknowledged before a commissioned Notary Public or the Office of the Clerk of Courts at the Palau Supreme Court [3].
  • Banking and revenue mandates: Commercial banks operating in Koror (including FDIC-insured U.S. branch banks and local institutions) frequently require their own internal power-of-attorney or joint signatory forms in addition to a general notarized Power of Attorney [3] [5]. Arrange for your family member to sign bank mandate forms and update account beneficiary designations while able to appear in person or verify identity directly with bank officers.
  • Cross-border authentication (Apostille): Because the Republic of Palau is a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, a Power of Attorney executed in Palau for use in the United States or another Apostille jurisdiction (or executed abroad for use in Palau) should be authenticated with an Apostille through the Ministry of State or the Palau Supreme Court Clerk of Courts [3] [5].

steps.title: Activate Disability Benefits, Medical Savings Accounts, and Caregiver Support
steps.html:
• Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) pension: If the life-limiting illness prevents your family member from engaging in substantial gainful employment and is expected to last at least 12 months or result in death, file a disability pension claim with the Republic of Palau Social Security Administration in Koror (41 PNC) [4]. Once certified by a medical examination from a physician at Belau National Hospital and approved by the Social Security Board, the contributor receives a monthly disability benefit calculated under the statutory benefit formula [1] [4].
  • Civil Service Pension Plan and public assistance grants: If your family member is a current or former public servant, check eligibility for occupational or non-occupational disability retirement with the Civil Service Pension Plan, and verify whether severe functional impairment qualifies for monthly severe-disability or home-bound assistance grants administered in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Human Services [1] [4].
  • Statutory sick leave and family caregiver leave: Formal-sector and national government employees in Palau should coordinate accumulated paid sick leave and annual leave with their employer, or apply for unpaid family medical caregiver leave supported by a medical certificate from Belau National Hospital [1].

steps.title: Organize Wills, Customary Property Dispositions (Telungalek), and Vital Records
steps.html:
• Executing a valid Will under 25 PNC: Under Title 25 of the Palau National Code (25 PNC, Decedents' Estates) overseen by the Palau Supreme Court, a person of sound mind aged 18 or older may execute a written Last Will and Testament signed by the testator in the presence of at least two competent attesting witnesses [3]. Executing a clear written will while capacity is intact minimizes post-death disputes over individually owned land, leaseholds, business shares, and personal property [3].
  • Aligning statutory wills with Palauan customary obligations (Siukang) and constitutional land rules: Under Article XIII, Section 8 of the Constitution of the Republic of Palau and 39 PNC, only Palauan citizens may hold fee-simple title to land in Palau [3]. Because clan and lineage land (Telungalek and Kebliil property) is governed by customary tenure whereas individual land listed on a Certificate of Title issued by the Land Court can be devised to Palauan citizen heirs by will or recorded deed of transfer, it is advisable for your family member to clarify their wishes with senior lineage members (Rubak) and record any lifetime land transfers or directives with the Palau Supreme Court and the Land Court [3].
  • Consolidating civil status and beneficiary records: Verify that your family member's birth certificate, marriage certificate, children's birth records, and passport are up to date with the Vital Statistics Office at the Ministry of Health and Human Services and the Office of the Clerk of Courts at the Palau Supreme Court (34 PNC § 4005) [1] [2] [3], and update named beneficiaries on accounts with the Republic of Palau Social Security Administration and commercial insurers [4].

3. Durable Power of Attorney & bank mandatesBefore any decline in legal capacityNotary Public / Palau Supreme Court (Clerk of Courts) & commercial banks
4. Social Security Disability pension claimUpon medical certification of inability to workRepublic of Palau Social Security Administration
5. Will execution, land titles & vital recordsWhile capacity is intactPalau Supreme Court (Trial Division / Land Court) & Ministry of State

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Papua New Guinea: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Papua New Guinea: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Papua New Guinea: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death of your family member in Papua New Guinea. Navigating medical death certification, civil death registration (NID), funeral or domestic/international repatriation formalities, superannuation survivor claims, and estate probate under Papua New Guinean statutory and customary law involves several distinct public authorities. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or clinical deaths: When a death occurs in a public or church-run hospital in Papua New Guinea (such as Port Moresby General Hospital or a Provincial Health Authority hospital overseen by the National Department of Health), the attending medical practitioner examines the deceased and issues the official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD) [1] [2] [6]. Keep the signed original and make certified copies, as the hospital mortuary, the civil registry, and superannuation funds require it.
  • Deaths at home or in a rural village (natural causes): If your family member died at home or in a rural community from natural causes without a doctor in attendance, notify the nearest health center or community health officer under the National Department of Health or the local ward recorder so a clinical or community death notification record can be completed for civil registration [1] [2] [6].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or unexplained deaths: If the death was sudden, accidental, or occurred under unclear circumstances, notify the Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary (RPNGC) immediately before moving the body [1] [2]. Police refer the case to the Coroner under the Coroners Act (Chapter 32), who directs a medico-legal post-mortem examination at an authorized hospital mortuary and issues a Coroner's Certificate for burial and release of the remains [1] [2] [6].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry (PNGCIR)
steps.html:
• Competent civil registry authority: Vital events in Papua New Guinea are governed by the Civil Registration Act 1963 (Chapter 304), as amended by the Civil Registration (Amendment) Act 2014, and administered by the Registrar-General at the Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry (which also manages the National Identification NID project) in Port Moresby and provincial capitals [1] [2].
  • Statutory registration deadline and fees: Under the Civil Registration Act 1963 (Chapter 304), the nearest adult relative present at the death or attending during the last illness (or the occupier of the premises) must submit the Death Registration Form within 28 days of the date of death (extended up to 3 months in remote districts) [1] [2]. Death registration and the issuance of the initial official Death Certificate by the Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry are free of statutory charge [2].
  • Required documents: Present the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or Coroner's Certificate), the burial or mortuary slip, the deceased's National Identification (NID) card or birth certificate, and the informant's NID card or passport at the nearest Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry office to obtain official certified Death Certificates [1] [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Provincial Transfer, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local burial, cremation, or inter-provincial transfer (Haus Krai): To arrange burial at an urban cemetery (such as 9-Mile Cemetery in Port Moresby) or domestic air cargo transfer of the casket to a home province for customary funeral rites (Haus Krai), engage a licensed funeral director or the hospital mortuary and present the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or Coroner's release order) together with mortuary clearance from the National Department of Health [1] [2] [6].
  • International repatriation of remains: If the deceased was a foreign national or a Papua New Guinean citizen whose remains must be repatriated abroad (typically via Jacksons International Airport in Port Moresby), the licensed funeral provider must obtain an official Death Certificate, an Embalming Certificate, a Hermetic Coffin Sealing Certificate, a Public Health Quarantine Export Permit from the National Department of Health, customs export clearance, and a consular No-Objection Certificate from the relevant foreign High Commission or Embassy in Port Moresby [2] [6].
  • Document authentication and consular legalization: Because Papua New Guinea is not currently a contracting party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, official Papua New Guinean Death Certificates and National Court probate grants intended for use in foreign jurisdictions must be authenticated by the Protocol and Consular Division of the Department of Foreign Affairs in Port Moresby and legalized by the embassy or high commission of the destination country [1] [2].

steps.title: Claim Mandatory Superannuation Survivor Benefits and Notify Financial Authorities
steps.html:
• Mandatory superannuation death benefits (Nambawan Super and Nasfund): Under the Superannuation (General Provisions) Act 2000, formal-sector employees in Papua New Guinea contribute to an authorized mandatory superannuation fund, principally Nambawan Super Limited (covering public servants and private contributors) or the National Superannuation Fund (Nasfund) [4] [5]. Upon a member's death, surviving nominated beneficiaries (Section 89 Nominees) file a Death Claim with Nambawan Super Limited or Nasfund to receive a lump-sum payout of the deceased's accumulated member and employer contributions plus any applicable group life insurance death benefit [4] [5].
  • Workers' compensation and public service entitlements: If the death resulted from a work-related accident or occupational illness, notify the employer and the Office of Workers' Compensation to claim statutory survivor compensation [4]. For public servants, notify the employing government department and the Department of Personnel Management to process final salary, accrued leave, and state death gratuity entitlements [4] [5].
  • Tax and banking notifications: Present the official Death Certificate and NID records to commercial banks (BSP Financial Group, Kina Bank, or Westpac PNG) to freeze sole accounts and verify estate release procedures, and notify the Internal Revenue Commission if the deceased held an active business Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) [3] [4].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Probate, Public Curator, and Customary Succession (Kastom)
steps.html:
• Probate and Letters of Administration before the National Court of Justice: Estate succession in Papua New Guinea is governed by the Wills, Probate and Administration Act 1966 (Chapter 291) [3]. Where the deceased left a valid formal will (Testate Estate), the executor applies to the National Court of Justice (Probate Jurisdiction) for a Grant of Probate [3]. Where a person dies without a written will (Intestate Estate) leaving non-customary assets (such as bank balances above small-estate limits, State land leases, or company shares), the surviving spouse or next of kin applies to the National Court of Justice for Letters of Administration, or the estate may be administered through the Office of the Public Curator [3].
  • Statutory distinction between modern assets and customary (Kastom) property: Under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act 1966 (Chapter 291), customary land and traditional property owned by a citizen of Papua New Guinea are excluded from statutory wills and intestacy distributions and instead devolve strictly according to local customary law (Kastom - matrilineal or patrilineal clan rules), with disputes resolved through Village Courts and Provincial Land Courts rather than National Court probate [3].
  • No formal inheritance tax and cross-border coordination: Papua New Guinea does not levy a separate estate or inheritance tax on property passing to heirs upon death, although stamp duties and tax clearances apply to transfers of State leaseholds or corporate shares [3] [4]. Heirs living abroad may authorize a lawyer in Papua New Guinea to apply for resealing of a foreign probate grant or Letters of Administration before the National Court of Justice using a notarized and consulate-legalized Power of Attorney [2] [3].
StepDeadlineAuthority
1. Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD)Immediately upon deathNational Department of Health (Hospital) or Coroner
2. Civil death registration (NID / PNGCIR)Within 28 days (up to 3 months in remote areas)Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry
3. Burial, provincial transfer, or repatriationPrior to burial or domestic/international flightNational Department of Health & Department of Foreign Affairs
4. Superannuation death claimPromptly after obtaining Death Certificate & NIDNambawan Super Limited / Nasfund
5. Probate, Public Curator, or customary settlementFollowing funeral / Haus KraiNational Court of Justice (Probate) & Office of the Public Curator

closingQuestion: To help us tailor these steps to your situation, did the death occur in Port Moresby or another province of Papua New Guinea, and was your family member a member of Nambawan Super Limited or Nasfund or a foreign national whose remains or documents need to be sent abroad?

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Papua New Guinea: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Papua New Guinea: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Papua New Guinea: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: We understand that managing an advanced or life-limiting illness for your family member in Papua New Guinea requires timely medical, legal, and administrative preparation. Taking structured steps while your family member retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity ensures that specialist hospital and palliative care, medical consent preferences, powers of attorney, mandatory superannuation incapacity benefits, and statutory and customary estate records are properly arranged. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Coordinate Specialist Hospital, Palliative Care, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Hospital and palliative care services: Coordinate oncology, chronic-disease, and supportive symptom-management care through Port Moresby General Hospital, Angau Memorial Provincial Hospital in Lae, or the relevant Provincial Health Authority hospital overseen by the National Department of Health, alongside accredited church health services and cancer support clinics [6]. Ask the attending specialist physician for a comprehensive written clinical summary (Medical Diagnosis and Prognosis Report) and an outpatient pain-relief and home-care plan [6].
  • Public health fee policies and private medical insurance: Public hospitals under the National Department of Health provide subsidized inpatient and outpatient care for citizens, while employees in the public service or formal corporate sector may also hold group medical and critical-illness insurance (such as through Nambawan Super health partners, BSP Life, or Pacific Assurance Group) [4] [5] [6]. Contact any private health insurer early to pre-authorize inpatient treatment or overseas medical evacuation if required.

steps.title: Record Advance Healthcare Preferences and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Informed consent and comfort-focused care goals: Under the clinical governance standards of the National Department of Health and common-law principles recognized by the National Court of Justice, an adult patient who retains full mental capacity has the right to give or withhold informed consent to invasive medical or surgical interventions and to request comfort-focused palliative treatment [3] [6].
  • Written Advance Care Directive and Medical Proxy: Although Papua New Guinea does not have a standalone living-will statute, your family member can sign a written Advance Care Directive and Medical Proxy statement while mentally competent, naming a primary adult family representative (Next of Kin / Designated Medical Decision-Maker) and an alternate to consult with hospital doctors if your family member later becomes unable to communicate [3] [6].
  • Clinical capacity verification in hospital records: Request that the attending medical officer at the Provincial Health Authority hospital record a dated note in the clinical chart confirming that your family member is alert, oriented, and of sound mind at the time they sign medical directives, powers of attorney, or superannuation forms [3] [6].

steps.title: Execute Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates While Capacity Is Intact
steps.html:
• Formal Power of Attorney: Under Papua New Guinean common-law agency rules and statutory property legislation overseen by the National Court of Justice, an adult with full legal capacity may execute a written Power of Attorney (Deed of Power of Attorney) witnessed by a qualified Lawyer or a Commissioner for Oaths appointing a trusted representative to manage financial affairs, business tax filings, and personal property [3]. If the Power of Attorney authorizes dealings with registered State land leases, it must also be lodged for registration with the Registrar of Titles at the Department of Lands and Physical Planning [3].
  • Commercial bank mandates: Commercial banks operating in Papua New Guinea (BSP Financial Group, Kina Bank, and Westpac PNG) generally require account holders to sign the bank's own third-party signatory or mandate form in person (or via verified hospital visit) accompanied by valid National Identification (NID) cards [2] [3]. Arrange joint or authorized signatory access while your family member is able to verify their identity directly.
  • Cross-border document legalization: Because Papua New Guinea is not a contracting party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, any Power of Attorney executed in Papua New Guinea for use abroad (or executed outside Papua New Guinea for use before local banks or the National Court of Justice) must be notarized and authenticated through the Department of Foreign Affairs and the relevant foreign embassy or High Commission in Port Moresby [1] [2] [3].

steps.title: Activate Superannuation Medical Incapacity Withdrawals and Leave Benefits
steps.html:
• Total and Permanent Incapacity superannuation claim (Nambawan Super and Nasfund): Under the Superannuation (General Provisions) Act 2000, contributors to Nambawan Super Limited or the National Superannuation Fund (Nasfund) who become permanently and totally incapacitated by a serious or terminal illness (physical or mental incapacity preventing the member from ever engaging in gainful employment) can apply for an early full withdrawal of their accumulated superannuation balance [4] [5]. The application requires a completed Medical Incapacity Claim Form supported by formal medical certificates from two registered medical practitioners approved by the National Department of Health [4] [5] [6].
  • Paid sick leave and public service medical retirement: Under the Employment Act 1978 and Public Service General Orders, formal-sector employees are entitled to paid sick leave and accrued recreational or long-service leave upon presentation of a medical certificate [4]. Public servants facing permanent life-limiting illness may also undergo a National Department of Health Medical Board assessment (medical boarding-out) to access early medical retirement entitlements through their department and Nambawan Super Limited [4] [5] [6].

steps.title: Organize Wills, Superannuation Nominations, NID Records, and Customary Property
steps.html:
• Executing a statutory Will under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act 1966: Under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act 1966 (Chapter 291), an adult of sound mind may execute a formal written Will signed by the testator in the presence of two independent attesting witnesses (neither of whom should be a beneficiary or spouse of a beneficiary) [3]. A statutory Will governs modern non-customary assets (such as bank accounts, vehicles, company shares, and registered State land leases) that otherwise pass under statutory intestacy rules administered by the National Court of Justice or the Office of the Public Curator [3].
  • Distinguishing customary (Kastom) land and property: Under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act 1966 (Chapter 291), customary land and traditional clan property in Papua New Guinea cannot be devised by a statutory Will contrary to local custom; instead, they pass according to the applicable matrilineal or patrilineal clan rules (Kastom) [3]. It is advisable for your family member to record clear family understandings with clan elders regarding customary obligations alongside their written statutory Will for modern assets [3].
  • Updating Superannuation Beneficiary Nominations (Section 89 Nominees) and NID registration: Because superannuation funds in Nambawan Super Limited and Nasfund are disbursed directly to the member's registered nominees outside court probate, your family member should review and sign an updated Superannuation Nomination Form while capacity is intact [4] [5]. At the same time, verify that your family member, their spouse, and all nominated children hold official Birth Certificates, Marriage Certificates, and National Identification (NID) cards issued by the Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry under the Civil Registration Act 1963 (Chapter 304), as valid NID identification is strictly required by superannuation boards and banks to release funds [1] [2] [5].

3. Power of Attorney & bank signatory mandatesBefore any decline in legal capacityLawyer / Commissioner for Oaths & commercial banks
4. Superannuation medical incapacity claimUpon certification by two medical practitionersNambawan Super Limited / Nasfund
5. Statutory Will, Superannuation Nomination & NIDWhile capacity is intactNational Court of Justice, Nambawan Super Limited & Papua New Guinea Civil and Identity Registry

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Pakistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Pakistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Pakistan: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences to you and your family following the death of your family member in Pakistan. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps to manage medical death certification, civil registration, funeral or international repatriation formalities, survivor benefit claims, and estate administration under Pakistani law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or clinical deaths: When a death occurs in a public or private hospital in Pakistan, the attending medical officer issues an official Hospital Death Certificate (Cause of Death Certificate) recording the deceased's full name, Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) number, date and time of death, and clinical cause of death [1]. You should request multiple signed and stamped copies from the hospital administration desk before moving the deceased.
  • Deaths at home (natural causes): If your family member died at home from natural causes, a registered medical practitioner (MBBS physician) who treated the deceased or examined the body must issue a medical cause of death certificate [1]. Where no physician attended the deceased in rural or residential areas, local Union Council or Cantonment Board rules allow two adult witnesses or a graveyard management receipt to support local verification [1].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or suspicious deaths: If the death was sudden, accidental, or unattended, you must immediately notify the local police station. Under Section 174 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the police prepare an inquest report and transfer the body to a government hospital Police Surgeon or Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) for a post-mortem examination before issuing a Medico-Legal Certificate and police clearance for burial or transport [1].

steps.title: Register the Death and Obtain Official NADRA Death Certificates
steps.html:
• Where and when to register: Civil death registration in Pakistan is conducted at the local Union Council, Municipal Committee, Metropolitan Corporation, or Cantonment Board where the death occurred or where the deceased held permanent residence, feeding into the Civil Registration Management System (CRMS) maintained by the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) [1]. Standard registration should be completed within 60 days of the death; late registration after the statutory window requires an affidavit, late fee, and administrative approval from the local municipal or district authority [1].
  • Required documents for registration: A close family member (applicant) must submit the original hospital death certificate or graveyard burial slip, copies of the deceased's CNIC, the applicant's valid CNIC, and an official registration application form [1].
  • CNIC cancellation and updated Family Registration Certificate (FRC): Once the local Union Council or Cantonment Board issues the computerized NADRA Death Registration Certificate, you must visit a NADRA Registration Center (or use the Pak ID platform) to formally cancel the deceased's CNIC and obtain an updated Family Registration Certificate (FRC) [1, 2]. Both the NADRA Death Certificate and the updated FRC are mandatory prerequisites for all banking, pension, and succession procedures in Pakistan [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local burial or cremation permits: In Pakistan, burial is arranged through municipal graveyards, Cantonment Board cemeteries, or community welfare organizations (such as Edhi Foundation or Chhipa Welfare Association), while minority communities arrange burial or cremation at designated municipal grounds [1]. The graveyard or crematorium supervisor requires the hospital cause of death certificate (and police No Objection Certificate in medico-legal cases) and issues a burial or cremation receipt needed for civil registration [1].
  • International repatriation of human remains: If the deceased is to be repatriated abroad, a licensed funeral and cargo provider must arrange embalming at an authorized hospital mortuary, a non-infectious disease and hermetically sealed coffin certificate, a police No Objection Certificate (NOC), and airport health and customs clearance [1, 3].
  • Apostille and consular legalization: If your family member was a foreign national, you must notify their embassy or high commission in Islamabad or Karachi to obtain a consular mortuary passport or NOC. For Pakistani NADRA death certificates that must be used abroad, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) provides official document attestation and Hague Apostille certification through its camp offices and authorized courier desks [3].

steps.title: Notify Pension, Social Security, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Private-sector survivor pension and grants (EOBI): If the deceased was an insured private-sector worker or pensioner registered with the Employees' Old-Age Benefits Institution (EOBI), eligible survivors can claim a monthly Survivor's Pension or an Old-Age Grant by submitting the NADRA Death Certificate, CNIC cancellation slip, and updated FRC to the regional EOBI office [4].
  • Federal and provincial civil service benefits: If the deceased was a serving or retired civil servant, the family should notify the parent department, the Accountant General Pakistan Revenues (AGPR), or the relevant provincial accounts office to claim the family pension, death gratuity, benevolent fund grant, and official Assistance Package for Families of Deceased Government Employees [2, 5].
  • Tax and banking notifications (FBR and commercial banks): You must notify all Pakistani banks where the deceased held accounts or lockers; banks freeze sole accounts upon death notification until a valid Succession Certificate is presented [1]. The legal representative should also notify the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to settle final income tax returns and update the deceased's tax registration status [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Succession Certificates, and Cross-Border Assets
steps.html:
• Succession Certificates and Letters of Administration via NADRA: Under the Letters of Administration and Succession Certificates Act, 2020, legal heirs in undisputed cases no longer need to file lengthy civil court petitions. Instead, heirs apply directly through a NADRA Succession Facilitation Unit for a Succession Certificate (covering movable assets such as bank accounts, shares, and saving schemes) or Letters of Administration (covering immovable real estate) [1, 3].
  • Biometric verification and 14-day public notice: The NADRA succession process requires submitting the NADRA Death Certificate, the updated FRC showing all legal heirs, asset ownership documents, a 14-day public newspaper notice to confirm no objections exist, and biometric verification of every legal heir [1, 3].
  • Overseas heirs and contested estates: If any legal heir resides outside Pakistan, biometric verification can be completed remotely through Pakistan Missions Abroad coordinated with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) or by executing a digital Power of Attorney [3]. If a dispute arises among heirs or if there is a contested will, NADRA refers the matter to the competent Civil or High Court for formal judicial probate or succession proceedings [1]. Pakistan does not currently levy a separate federal inheritance or estate duty on inherited assets, though municipal property transfer fees and capital value taxes may apply when mutating real estate titles [5].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Pakistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Pakistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Pakistan: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Pakistan is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, taking timely medical, legal, and administrative steps while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity helps protect their care preferences and financial affairs. Below, we set out the five key steps to coordinate palliative care, medical representation, powers of attorney, social security support, and estate organization in Pakistan.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Hospital palliative care and oncology units: Specialized palliative care, pain management, and supportive symptom relief in Pakistan are delivered through major tertiary public and charitable hospitals (such as Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, Aga Khan University Hospital, and federal hospitals overseen by the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination (NHSRC)) [1]. You should ask the primary specialist for a comprehensive clinical summary and a written home-care and pain-management protocol.
  • Public and private health coverage: For eligible families registered under federal or provincial social health protection schemes (such as the Sehat Sahulat Program), inpatient treatment and critical-illness care at empaneled public and private hospitals are covered up to statutory limits under frameworks coordinated with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination (NHSRC) [1]. If your family member holds private health or critical-illness insurance, notify the insurer early to obtain pre-authorization for inpatient or home nursing care.
  • Home nursing and clinical continuity: Keeping an organized medical file at home - including diagnostic reports, prescriptions for controlled analgesics, and an attending physician's contact details - ensures uninterrupted symptom management and facilitates medical documentation if an emergency occurs [1].

steps.title: Record Medical Treatment Preferences and Designate a Healthcare Representative
steps.html:
• Written treatment preferences and informed consent: Pakistan does not currently have a standalone federal statute governing statutory living wills for all provinces, so medical consent and end-of-life care decisions are governed by hospital clinical ethics policies, constitutional protections of dignity, and physician-family consultation [1]. While your family member has full mental capacity, it is advisable to consider recording their written preferences regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), mechanical ventilation, intensive care admission, and comfort-focused care.
  • Designating a primary medical spokesperson: Your family member should formally name a trusted adult relative as their primary medical representative in their hospital admission records and in a notarized declaration witnessed by two adults [1] [2]. Having a clear written designation prevents disagreements among extended relatives when urgent clinical decisions are required.
  • Hospital ethics committee alignment: Provide signed copies of your family member's care preferences to the treating consultant and hospital medical record department so that any Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) or palliative-only care order is properly documented in the clinical chart by the medical team [1].

steps.title: Execute Financial and Legal Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• General or Special Power of Attorney (Mukhtar-nama): Under the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882 and the Registration Act, 1908, your family member can execute a Special Power of Attorney (for specific banking or administrative acts) or a General Power of Attorney (for broader asset and property management) while they retain full mental capacity [2]. Any Power of Attorney authorizing the sale, mortgage, or transfer of immovable real estate in Pakistan must be executed on appropriate stamp paper, witnessed by two adults, and compulsorily registered with the local Sub-Registrar of Properties [2].
  • Digital Power of Attorney for overseas relatives: If the person granting or receiving the mandate is abroad, the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) operate an official online Digital Power of Attorney portal featuring biometric verification and consular video interviews [2] [3].
  • Bank account mandates and biometric exemptions: Because Pakistani banks require NADRA biometric verification for account operations, your family member should visit or contact their bank while able to register a formal bank mandate, joint signing authority, or medical exemption for thumb-impression verification, and ensure their pensioner verification status with the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) is up to date [3].

steps.title: Activate Disability, Invalidity, and Caregiver Support Benefits
steps.html:
• Private-sector Invalidity Pension (EOBI): If your family member is an insured private-sector employee who becomes permanently incapacitated due to severe illness, they can apply for an Invalidity Pension or Old-Age Grant through the Employees' Old-Age Benefits Institution (EOBI), supported by a medical board assessment confirming permanent inability to work [4].
  • Disability assessment and social protection: Under federal and provincial disability rights frameworks coordinated with the Ministry of Human Rights (MOHR) and social welfare departments, individuals with severe functional impairment can undergo assessment by a District Medical Board to obtain a Special CNIC (disability emblem) through NADRA, unlocking public medical concessions and social protection support [5].
  • Civil service medical boarding and leave: If the ill person is a federal or provincial government employee, they may apply for medical leave, a medical board invalidation pension, or medical reimbursement grants under civil service rules, while employed family caregivers can request statutory casual, earned, or compassionate leave from their employer [1] [4].

steps.title: Review Wills, Civil Records, and Cross-Border Estate Documents
steps.html:
• Reviewing wills (Wasiyat) and succession rules: In Pakistan, succession for Muslims is governed by Islamic personal law (Shariat Application Acts), under which a testator may generally bequeath up to one-third of their net estate by will (Wasiyat) to non-heirs without the consent of legal heirs, while the remaining two-thirds passes according to fixed Quranic shares; non-Muslim citizens are governed by the Succession Act, 1925 [2] [3]. Preparing a clear, witnessed written will and a complete inventory of assets prevents disputes.
  • Verifying NADRA Family Registration Certificate (FRC): While your family member has full capacity, obtain and verify an updated Family Registration Certificate (FRC) from the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) to ensure that all spouses, children, and parents are accurately linked by CNIC number [3] [6]. Discrepancies in NADRA family tree records are the single most common cause of delay in post-death NADRA Succession Certificate applications [6].
  • Organizing property titles and cross-border nominations: Gather original property title deeds (fard, registry, allotment letters), bank account statements, Central Depository Company (CDC) share details, and National Savings certificates, and update nominee designations on life insurance and provident funds [2] [6]. If assets or family members are located outside Pakistan, coordinate cross-border powers of attorney and Apostille legalization through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) [2].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Samoa: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Samoa: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Samoa: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences to you and your family following the death of your family member in Samoa. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps to manage medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral or international repatriation arrangements, survivor benefit notifications, and estate administration under Samoan law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or clinical deaths: When a death occurs at Tupua Tamasese Meaole (TTM) Hospital in Motootua (Apia), Malietoa Tanumafili II Hospital in Tuasivi (Savai'i), or a district health facility operated under the Ministry of Health, the attending medical practitioner examines the body and issues an official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Death Notification Form) [1, 2]. You should obtain signed copies from the hospital records office before transferring the deceased to a mortuary.
  • Deaths at home or in a village (natural causes): If your family member died at home or in a village in Upolu or Savai'i from natural causes without a doctor present, you must notify a registered medical practitioner or the nearest district health center to examine the body, and obtain written confirmation from the village mayor (Pulenu'u / Sui o le Nu'u) and the officiating church minister [1, 2].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or unexplained deaths: Under the Coroners Ordinance 1959 and court oversight administered by the Ministry of Justice and Courts Administration (MJCA), any sudden, violent, accidental, or unexplained death must be reported immediately to the Samoa Police Service [3]. The police refer the case to the Coroner, who may order a forensic post-mortem examination at the national hospital mortuary before issuing a coroner's authorization for burial or release of the body [1, 3].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Samoa Bureau of Statistics
steps.html:
• Statutory registration authority and 14-day deadline: Under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 2002, all deaths in Samoa must be officially registered with the Births, Deaths and Marriages (BDM) Division of the Samoa Bureau of Statistics (SBS), located at the Mulinu'u or Apia government complex in Upolu or the Salelologa branch office in Savai'i [1, 2]. Statutory registration must be completed within 14 days of the date of death [2].
  • Required documents for civil registration: To register the death and obtain an official Samoan Death Certificate, an immediate family member or funeral director must submit the completed Death Registration Form, the original hospital Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or village Pulenu'u and church minister confirmation for community deaths), the deceased's birth certificate or passport, and valid photo identification of the informant [1, 2].
  • Late registration requirements: If a death is registered after the statutory window, the Registrar General at the Samoa Bureau of Statistics (SBS) requires supplemental supporting evidence, such as hospital archive verification, church burial records, a statutory declaration explaining the delay, and payment of the prescribed late registration fee [2].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local funeral, customary burial, or cemetery permits: Families in Samoa typically coordinate mortuary care, embalming, and casket preparation through a licensed funeral home in Apia (such as Sefo's Funeral Home or Ligaliga Funeral Home) [1]. Burials may take place at public cemeteries or on approved family land in accordance with village council rules and public health sanitation regulations enforced by the Ministry of Health [4].
  • International repatriation of human remains: If the deceased is to be repatriated overseas (for example, to New Zealand, Australia, or the United States), the licensed funeral provider must arrange full arterial embalming, a hermetically sealed zinc-lined or metal shipping casket, a Certificate of Non-Contagious Disease and Embalming Certificate from the Ministry of Health, an official Death Certificate from the Samoa Bureau of Statistics (SBS), and customs and aviation security clearance at Faleolo International Airport [1, 4].
  • Apostille legalization and foreign consular notification: If your family member was a foreign citizen, notify their embassy or high commission in Apia immediately to obtain a consular mortuary certificate. Because Samoa is a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, Samoan Death Certificates destined for use abroad can receive an official Apostille certificate from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Apia [1, 2].

steps.title: Notify Provident Fund, Pension, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF) death benefits: If your family member was a contributor or pensioner with the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF), notify the fund's main office in Apia or Savai'i promptly [5]. Surviving nominated beneficiaries or legal dependents can claim the deceased member's accumulated contribution balance and any applicable Special Death Benefit or funeral assistance grant by submitting the official SBS Death Certificate, marriage or birth certificates proving relationship, and valid identification [5].
  • Senior Citizens Benefit Fund (SCBF) notification: If the deceased was aged 65 or older and receiving the government monthly pension under the Senior Citizens Benefit Fund administered by the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF), the family must report the death so that monthly pension payments are closed and any final month entitlement is reconciled [5].
  • Banking and tax notifications: Present certified copies of the SBS Death Certificate to all commercial banks in Samoa (such as Bank South Pacific, ANZ Samoa, or National Bank of Samoa) and the Ministry for Revenue (Inland Revenue Services) to freeze sole bank accounts, settle any outstanding income or business tax obligations, and cancel official identity credentials [2, 3].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Probate, and Succession in Samoa
steps.html:
• Probate and Letters of Administration under the Administration Act 1975: Estate administration in Samoa is governed by the Wills Act 1975 and the Administration Act 1975 [6]. Where the deceased left a valid written will, the named executor must apply to the Supreme Court of Samoa - administered by the Ministry of Justice and Courts Administration (MJCA) - for a Grant of Probate [3, 6]. If the deceased died intestate (without a will), the surviving spouse or next-of-kin must petition the Supreme Court for Letters of Administration, or the estate may be administered through the Public Trust Office [3, 6].
  • Freehold property vs. customary land rules: Under Article 102 of the Constitution of Samoa and the Administration Act 1975, only freehold land and personal property (such as bank accounts, vehicles, shares, and business assets) form part of the probate estate distributed under a will or statutory intestacy rules [6]. Customary land cannot be devised by will and is governed separately by Samoan custom and usage and the Land and Titles Court under the Ministry of Justice and Courts Administration (MJCA) [3, 6].
  • Taxation and cross-border coordination: Samoa does not levy a separate inheritance or estate duty on deceased estates, though court probate filing fees and property transfer registration fees apply [3, 6]. If heirs reside overseas (such as in New Zealand, Australia, or the United States) or if foreign grants of probate must be recognized in Samoa, the Supreme Court can reseal Commonwealth probate grants or accept notarized and Apostilled affidavits from overseas executors [3, 6].

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Samoa: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Samoa: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Samoa: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Samoa is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, putting medical, legal, and financial arrangements in place while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity ensures their wishes are respected and avoids avoidable court delays. Below, we set out the five key steps to coordinate palliative care, medical representation, powers of attorney, social security support, and estate preparation in Samoa.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Public hospital and community palliative care: In Samoa, inpatient specialist care, oncology support, and symptom management are coordinated through Tupua Tamasese Meaole (TTM) Hospital in Motootua (Apia), Malietoa Tanumafili II Hospital in Tuasivi (Savai'i), and rural district hospitals operating under the Ministry of Health [1]. Families should request a formal clinical summary, pain-relief prescription plan, and referral to community nursing or charitable home-care support (such as the Samoa Cancer Society for oncology patients) [1].
  • Public healthcare concessions and overseas medical referral: Citizens and permanent residents aged 65 and over registered with the Senior Citizens Benefit Fund under the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF) receive free medical consultations, inpatient hospital care, and prescription pharmaceuticals at government health facilities, as well as free inter-island ferry travel between Upolu and Savai'i [2]. Where specialized palliative or clinical treatment is arranged through the Samoa Medical Treatment Scheme, referrals are coordinated with the Ministry of Health [1].
  • Maintaining clinical records at home: Keep an accessible folder containing the ill person's hospital discharge summaries, medication charts, and attending doctor's contact details so community nurses or visiting physicians can provide seamless symptom relief at home [1].

steps.title: Record Advance Care Preferences and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Written advance medical care statement: Samoa does not currently have a standalone statutory living will act, so clinical consent and end-of-life treatment decisions are governed by common-law principles of informed consent and health service regulations administered by the Ministry of Health [1]. While your family member retains full decision-making capacity, they should sign a written statement recording their preferences regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), artificial ventilation, intensive care interventions, and comfort-focused care.
  • Designating a primary healthcare proxy: Because extended family (aiga) consultations are central in Samoan medical settings, having the ill person explicitly name one primary medical spokesperson in their hospital chart and in a witnessed written document prevents uncertainty when urgent treatment decisions arise [1] [3].
  • Lodging directives with the treating team: Provide copies of the signed care statement and spokesperson designation to the attending consultant at TTM Hospital or the relevant district hospital so the medical team records these instructions directly in the clinical file [1].

steps.title: Execute Valid Financial Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• General or Specific Power of Attorney: Under Samoan property and contract law (including the Property Law Act 1952), an adult with full mental capacity may execute a Deed of Power of Attorney appointing a trusted relative or legal representative (attorney-in-fact) to manage bank accounts, pay bills, sign legal documents, and administer property in Samoa [3] [4]. The Power of Attorney should be drafted by a practicing lawyer or notary public in Samoa and signed in the presence of an adult witness.
  • Capacity and registration rules: Unless expressly structured and recognized under applicable statutory provisions, an ordinary Power of Attorney ceases to operate if the donor loses mental capacity; therefore, executing both a formal Power of Attorney and direct bank signing mandates while capacity is completely intact is essential [3] [4]. If the Power of Attorney authorizes dealings with freehold land leases or conveyances, it must be registered with the Land Registry [3].
  • Commercial bank mandates: Commercial banks in Samoa (such as Bank South Pacific, ANZ Samoa, and National Bank of Samoa) often require customers to sign the bank's own Third-Party Authority Form or convert an individual account into a joint signatory account in person while the account holder is able to attend the branch or verify identity [3].

steps.title: Activate Incapacity, Provident Fund, and Senior Citizen Benefits
steps.html:
• Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF) medical incapacity withdrawals: If your family member is a contributing or inactive member of the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF) and is certified by a recognized medical board or government specialist as permanently physically or mentally incapacitated from engaging in further employment, they can apply for an early medical incapacity withdrawal or pension payout while alive [2].
  • Senior Citizens Benefit Fund (SCBF) entitlements: If the ill person is aged 65 or older and a resident citizen or permanent resident of Samoa, ensure they are enrolled in the Senior Citizens Benefit Fund administered by the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF) to receive the monthly cash pension and public hospital healthcare exemptions [2]. If mobility limitations prevent the pensioner from collecting funds or updating details in person, an authorized representative can arrange home verification with SNPF officers [2].
  • Caregiver leave and workplace arrangements: Under the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013, employed family members caring for a seriously ill relative in Samoa can request paid sick/dependents leave, annual leave, or flexible compassionate leave arrangements through their employer [1] [3].

steps.title: Review Wills, Nominee Designations, Civil Records, and Customary vs. Freehold Assets
steps.html:
• Executing or updating a valid Will: Under the Wills Act 1975 and the Administration Act 1975, a valid Will in Samoa must be in writing and signed by the testator in the presence of at least two independent adult witnesses who are present at the same time and who are not beneficiaries (nor spouses of beneficiaries) under the Will [4]. Preparing a clear Will simplifies subsequent probate proceedings before the Supreme Court Division of the Ministry of Justice and Courts Administration (MJCA) [3] [4].
  • Distinguishing freehold property from customary land: When organizing estate documents under the Administration Act 1975, keep in mind that a Will can only dispose of freehold land, leasehold interests, and personal property (such as bank balances, business shares, and vehicles) [4]. Customary land and matai titles cannot be transferred by Will and remain subject to Samoan custom and usage under the jurisdiction of the Land and Titles Court within the Ministry of Justice and Courts Administration (MJCA) [3] [4].
  • Updating SNPF nominations and civil registry records: While your family member has full capacity, they should review and update their official beneficiary Nomination Form with the Samoa National Provident Fund (SNPF), as valid SNPF nominations allow benefits to be paid directly to named dependents [2]. Simultaneously, verify that birth certificates and marriage certificates are accurate and on file with the Births, Deaths and Marriages Division of the Samoa Bureau of Statistics (SBS) [5] [6]. If assets or family members are located in New Zealand, Australia, or the United States, coordinate separate local wills or Apostilled powers of attorney so cross-border assets can be managed without delay [3] [4].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Solomon Islands: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Solomon Islands: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Solomon Islands: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences to you and your family following the death of your family member in Solomon Islands. Below, we set out the five main official and practical steps to manage medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral or international repatriation arrangements, survivor benefit notifications, and estate administration under Solomon Islands law.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death
steps.html:
• Hospital or clinical deaths: When a death occurs at the National Referral Hospital (NRH) in Honiara, a provincial hospital (such as Kilu'ufi Hospital in Malaita, Gizo Hospital in Western Province, or Kirakira Hospital in Makira-Ulawa), or an Area Health Centre operated by the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS), the attending medical practitioner examines the body and issues an official Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD) [1] [2]. We suggest requesting multiple signed copies from the hospital medical records office before moving the deceased from the mortuary.
  • Deaths at home or in rural and outer-island villages (natural causes): If your family member died at home or in a rural community from natural causes without a doctor present, notify the nearest Rural Health Clinic or Area Health Centre under the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) so a registered nurse or medical officer can issue a clinical death notification, supplemented by written confirmation from the village chief, catechist, or officiating church minister [1] [3].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or unexplained deaths: Under the Death and Fire Inquiries Act (Cap. 7) and court oversight linked with the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA), any sudden, violent, accidental, or unexplained death must be reported immediately to the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force (RSIPF) [4]. Police officers refer the matter to a Magistrate acting as Coroner, who may direct a forensic post-mortem examination at the National Referral Hospital mortuary before authorizing release of the body for burial [1] [4].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Ministry of Home Affairs
steps.html:
• Statutory registration authority and deadline: Under the Births and Deaths (Registration) Act (Cap. 168), all deaths occurring in Solomon Islands must be registered with the Civil Registration Office (Office of the Registrar General of Births and Deaths) within the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in Honiara or through designated provincial civil registration officers [2] [3]. Families should submit the death notification within the statutory two-month (60-day) reporting window so the entry is recorded in the National Civil Registration Database without late-registration formalities [2] [3].
  • Required documents for civil registration: To register the death and obtain an official Solomon Islands Death Certificate, an immediate relative or informant must present the completed Death Registration Form, the original Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or rural health clinic and church/village leader verification for community deaths), the deceased's birth certificate, national voter ID, or passport, and valid photo identification of the informant [2] [3].
  • Late registration requirements: If a death is reported after twelve months from the date of death, the Registrar General at the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) requires corroborating hospital or church burial registers, a statutory declaration explaining the delay, and payment of the prescribed late registration fee [2] [3].

steps.title: Arrange Burial, Cremation, or International Repatriation
steps.html:
• Local burial permits and customary burial: For burials in Honiara (such as at Kola'a Ridge Cemetery or Fulisango Cemetery), families obtain a burial permit through the Honiara City Council Environmental Health Division upon presenting the medical certificate of death from the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) [1]. Many Solomon Islands families arrange domestic inter-island transport by ship or domestic aircraft to bury the deceased on ancestral customary land in their home province in accordance with local custom and public health sanitation rules [1] [2].
  • International repatriation of human remains: If the deceased was a foreign citizen or if remains must be repatriated abroad via Honiara International Airport (Henderson Field), the family and mortuary team at the National Referral Hospital must secure arterial embalming, a hermetically sealed zinc-lined shipping casket, a Certificate of Non-Contagious Disease and Embalming Certificate from the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS), an official Death Certificate from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), and customs and biosecurity export clearance [1] [2].
  • Consular legalization (non-Apostille jurisdiction): If your family member was a foreign national, notify their High Commission, Embassy, or Honorary Consul in Honiara immediately to obtain a consular mortuary transit permit. Because Solomon Islands is not a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, Solomon Islands Death Certificates intended for legal use overseas must undergo diplomatic authentication through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and External Trade in Honiara followed by consular legalization by the destination country's diplomatic mission [2] [4].

steps.title: Notify SINPF, Tax, and Banking Authorities
steps.html:
• Solomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF) death benefits: Under the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund Act (Cap. 109), if the deceased was an active or former contributor to the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF), surviving nominated beneficiaries or legal dependents should notify the SINPF head office in Honiara or a provincial branch office in Auki, Gizo, or Noro [5] [6]. Beneficiaries may claim the deceased member's full accumulated contribution balance together with the statutory Special Death Benefit grant by submitting the official Death Certificate, medical cause-of-death record, birth or marriage certificates proving relationship, and valid identification [5] [6].
  • Tax clearance and employer final settlements: Report the death to the Inland Revenue Division (IRD) of the Ministry of Finance and Treasury in Honiara to close the deceased's Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) and reconcile any final salary, business tax, or public service gratuity entitlements [2] [5].
  • Commercial bank notifications: Provide certified copies of the Death Certificate to all commercial banks and credit institutions where the deceased held accounts (such as Bank South Pacific, ANZ Solomon Islands, Bred Bank Solomon, or Pan Oceanic Bank) so sole accounts are frozen pending estate administration [4] [5].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Probate, and Succession in Solomon Islands
steps.html:
• Probate and Letters of Administration under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act (Cap. 33): Formal estate administration in Solomon Islands is governed by the Wills, Probate and Administration Act (Cap. 33) under the judicial framework connected with the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA) [4]. Where the deceased left a valid written Will, the named executor petitions the High Court of Solomon Islands in Honiara for a Grant of Probate; where the deceased died intestate (without a will), the surviving spouse or next-of-kin applies to the High Court for Letters of Administration, or the estate may be administered by the Public Trustee [4].
  • Registered property vs. customary land succession: Under the Land and Titles Act (Cap. 133), only perpetual estates, fixed-term estates (such as registered urban land leases in Honiara or provincial centers), bank balances, shares, and personal property pass through High Court probate or statutory intestacy rules [4]. Customary land cannot be alienated by ordinary will to non-customary holders and devolves strictly in accordance with local clan and tribal custom, with disputes heard by local chiefs, Local Courts, and the Customary Land Appeal Court under the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA) [4].
  • Summary table of key steps and authorities:
StepDeadlineAuthority
1. Medical Certificate of Cause of DeathImmediately after deathMinistry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) / NRH
2. Civil death registrationWithin 60 days (2 months)Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) Civil Registration Office
3. Burial permit or repatriation clearanceBefore burial or flightMinistry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) / Honiara City Council
4. Provident fund & tax notificationsPromptly after registrationSolomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF) / IRD
5. Grant of Probate / Letters of AdministrationBefore distributing estate assetsHigh Court of Solomon Islands / Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA)

title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Solomon Islands: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Solomon Islands: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Solomon Islands: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a family member in Solomon Islands is diagnosed with an advanced, life-limiting, or terminal illness, putting medical, legal, and financial arrangements in place while the ill person still retains full mental and legal decision-making capacity ensures their wishes are respected and prevents administrative delays. Below, we set out the five key steps to coordinate palliative care, medical representation, powers of attorney, provident fund incapacity entitlements, and estate preparation under Solomon Islands law.

steps.title: Coordinate Palliative Care, Home Nursing, and Health Coverage
steps.html:
• Public hospital and community palliative care: In Solomon Islands, specialist inpatient care, oncology symptom control, and pain management are coordinated through the National Referral Hospital (NRH) in Honiara, provincial hospitals (including Kilu'ufi Hospital in Malaita, Gizo Hospital in Western Province, and Kirakira Hospital in Makira-Ulawa), and church-supported hospitals (such as Good Samaritan Hospital in Guadalcanal and Helena Goldie Hospital in Munda) operating alongside the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) [1] [2]. We suggest requesting a written clinical summary, a symptom-relief medication schedule, and referrals to Area Health Centre nurses or the Solomon Islands Cancer Society for community-based support [1] [2].
  • Public health coverage and overseas medical referral: Public consultations, inpatient beds, and essential medicines at government clinics and hospitals under the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) are publicly subsidized for Solomon Islands citizens [1] [2]. Where specialized clinical care or diagnostic review abroad is under consideration, referrals are assessed by the National Medical Treatment Overseas Committee at the National Referral Hospital [1].
  • Maintaining clinical records at home: Keep an organized folder at home containing the ill person's hospital discharge summaries, medication charts, and attending physician contact details so visiting nurses or provincial medical officers can coordinate care seamlessly [1].

steps.title: Record Advance Care Preferences and Designate a Medical Representative
steps.html:
• Written advance medical care statement: Solomon Islands does not currently have a standalone statutory living will act, so clinical consent and life-sustaining treatment decisions are governed by common-law principles of informed consent and clinical governance guidelines administered by the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) [1]. While your family member retains full mental capacity, it is advisable for them to sign a dated written statement in the presence of two adult witnesses setting out their preferences regarding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), mechanical ventilation, intensive care transfers, and comfort-focused palliative care.
  • Designating a primary healthcare spokesperson: Because extended family (wantok) consultations are central in Solomon Islands medical settings, having the ill person explicitly nominate one primary medical spokesperson in their National Referral Hospital or provincial hospital chart avoids ambiguity if urgent clinical decisions arise after capacity declines [1] [3].
  • Lodging directives with the treating medical team: Provide signed copies of the care preferences statement and spokesperson designation to the attending consultant at the National Referral Hospital or relevant provincial hospital so they are placed directly in the patient's medical record [1].

steps.title: Execute Valid Financial Powers of Attorney and Bank Mandates
steps.html:
• General or Specific Power of Attorney: Under common-law agency and property principles applied in Solomon Islands alongside the Land and Titles Act (Cap. 133), an adult with full mental capacity may execute a formal Deed of Power of Attorney appointing a trusted relative or legal representative (attorney-in-fact) to manage bank accounts, pay household expenses, sign contracts, and administer property [3]. The Power of Attorney should be drafted with legal assistance (through a private legal practitioner or, where eligible, advice via agencies under the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA)) and executed before an authorized witness or Commissioner for Oaths [3].
  • Capacity and land registry filing rules: Because an ordinary common-law Power of Attorney ceases to operate if the donor loses mental capacity, it is advisable to execute both a formal Power of Attorney and direct bank third-party mandates while capacity is completely intact [3]. If the Power of Attorney authorizes any transfer, lease, or charge over a registered perpetual estate or fixed-term estate in land, it must be formally attested and registered with the Land Registry under the Land and Titles Act (Cap. 133) [3].
  • Commercial bank mandates: Commercial banks in Solomon Islands (such as Bank South Pacific, ANZ Solomon Islands, Bred Bank Solomon, and Pan Oceanic Bank) generally require account holders to complete the bank's own Third-Party Authority Form or add a joint signatory in person while the account holder is able to verify their identity [3].

steps.title: Activate SINPF Medical Incapacity Withdrawals and Workplace Support
steps.html:
• Solomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF) medical incapacity payout: Under the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund Act (Cap. 109), if your family member is a member of the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF) and is certified by two registered medical practitioners (or an approved medical board) as permanently physically or mentally incapacitated from ever engaging in further employment, they can apply to withdraw their full accumulated SINPF retirement balance while alive [4] [5]. Members aged 50 or older who have retired from employment may also apply for age-based withdrawal at the SINPF head office in Honiara or branch offices in Auki, Gizo, or Noro [4] [5].
  • Employee sickness and workplace entitlements: Under the Labour Act (Cap. 73) and Workmen's Compensation Act (Cap. 77), employed workers facing serious illness are entitled to statutory paid sick leave and, where an illness is work-related, statutory medical and incapacity compensation [5]. Family caregivers employed in the public or private sector should request compassionate leave, annual leave, or flexible care arrangements from their employer's human resources department.
  • Updating SINPF beneficiary nominations: While your family member retains full legal capacity, they should verify or submit an updated official Nomination Form directly with the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF) so that any remaining provident fund credits and entitlements are directed clearly to their chosen family beneficiaries [4] [5].

steps.title: Review Wills, Civil Registry Records, and Customary vs. Registered Property
steps.html:
• Executing or updating a valid Will: Under the Wills, Probate and Administration Act (Cap. 33), a valid Will in Solomon Islands must be in writing and signed by the testator in the presence of at least two independent adult witnesses present at the same time who are not beneficiaries (or spouses of beneficiaries) under the Will [3]. Having a properly executed Will streamlines future administration before the High Court of Solomon Islands and justice agencies linked with the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA) [3].
  • Distinguishing registered estates from customary land: Under the Land and Titles Act (Cap. 133), a written Will can dispose of personal property (bank accounts, vehicles, business shares) as well as registered perpetual estates and fixed-term estates (such as urban property leases in Honiara) [3]. Customary land remains governed by local clan and tribal custom and cannot be transferred outside customary succession rules by an ordinary statutory Will [3].
  • Verifying civil status documents and cross-border assets: Confirm that the ill person's birth certificate, marriage certificate, and children's birth records are accurately registered with the Civil Registration Office at the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in Honiara, as consistent civil registry records are essential for SINPF claims and High Court filings [6]. Because Solomon Islands is not a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, if family members or assets are located abroad (for example, in Australia, New Zealand, or Fiji), any cross-border power of attorney or property document must be notarized and legalized through diplomatic and consular channels.
  • Summary table of key steps and authorities:
StepDeadlineAuthority
1. Palliative care & clinical summaryUpon diagnosisMinistry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) / NRH
2. Written care preferences & medical proxyWhile capacity is intactMinistry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) / Treating hospital
3. Power of Attorney & bank mandatesWhile capacity is intactLegal practitioner / Commercial banks / Land Registry
4. Medical incapacity payout & nomination updateUpon medical certificationSolomon Islands National Provident Fund (SINPF)
5. Will execution & civil record checkWhile capacity is intactHigh Court / Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs (MJLA) / Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)
